#6553. Kale Salad With Lemon, Grana Padano, and Currants

In this simple, elegant salad, the spicy flavor of thinly sliced raw kale is offset by nutty Grana Padano cheese, bright lemon, and sweet-tart dried currants.

Global recipes, tastes, and trends—straight to your inbox.

To a large serving bowl, add the kale, Grana Padano, currants, oil, lemon juice, 1 teaspoon of salt, and ½ teaspoon of black pepper and toss thoroughly. Set aside to rest for 5–10 minutes, then toss again. Taste and add more cheese, salt, and/or black pepper if desired.

#6552. The New Bon Appétit Cooking App Is Here!

This exciting new tool is more than a digital version of our extensive archive of recipes. The app is designed to help you plan and pull off great meals, whether you’re a novice cook or a seasoned chef. You’ll be able to explore curated menu collections from our editors, personalize your homepage by noting dietary preferences, and save your favorites to build your own collection. It also includes videos from the BA Test Kitchen, teaching you techniques so every recipe comes out perfectly.

The new Bon Appétit app also puts recipes from our sister brands right at your fingertips. You’ll be able to access thousands of recipes from Epicurious, classics from Gourmet magazine, as well as excerpts from beloved chefs and cookbook authors including José Andrés and Samin Nosrat.

We hope our new app will inspire you to make many great meals.

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

Owen Hughes is a freelance writer and editor specializing in data and digital technologies. Previously a senior editor at ZDNET, Owen has been writing about tech for more than a decade, during which time he has covered everything from AI, cybersecurity and supercomputers to programming languages and public sector IT. Owen is particularly interested in the intersection of technology, life and work ­– in his previous roles at ZDNET and TechRepublic, he wrote extensively about business leadership, digital transformation and the evolving dynamics of remote work.

#6550. 12 Years Ago, This Jumbo Jet Vanished Without a Trace. New High-Tech Ocean Robots May Finally Reveal What Happened.

The 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 remains one of aviation’s greatest unsolved mysteries. Inside the latest high-stakes search to find the missing Boeing 777.

On January 2, 2018, from the port city of Durban in eastern South Africa, a ship departed at dusk. This was no vessel outfitted for a nighttime pleasure cruise. In fact, it looked downright strange. Its hull was a shade of prison-jumpsuit orange. Its bow was adorned with a large, flat platform resembling a helipad. Antennas, some pointy, some contained in two white domes, covered its superstructure. A crane was mounted on the ship’s stern. Belowdecks sat eight autonomous submersibles, each weighing about 4,000 pounds, or the equivalent of a Ford F-150. This ship was heading east, bound for a section of the southern Indian Ocean about 1,500 miles west of Australia. Its mission? To find the notorious Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

When MH370 took off from Kuala Lumpur on March 8, 2014, shortly before 1 a.m. local time, there was no indication it wouldn’t be a routine flight. But the Boeing 777-200ER never reached its destination, Beijing. Instead, after 39 minutes in the air, the jetliner disappeared from radar; about seven hours after that, it vanished altogether. Satellite communications analyzed afterward showed that MH370 had turned southward and continued on that course until it presumably exhausted its fuel supply and crashed in the Indian Ocean off the western seaboard of Australia.

An expansive search was quickly mounted, the largest ever for a missing plane. Some 60 ships and 50 aircraft from 26 countries participated, at a cost of more than $150 million. More than 46,000 square miles of Indian Ocean seabed were scanned over a three-year period.

But the plane was never located, and the question of MH370’s whereabouts set off a freneticism rivaled perhaps only by the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s fate on her final flight. In the decade-plus since the plane vanished, numerous and varied hypotheses have surfaced. The aircraft crashed somewhere else, some suggested. Others insisted the plane was shot out of the sky. So vexing was MH370’s disappearance that it even spawned a Netflix docuseries in 2023. Still others contend that, without a doubt, MH370 is on the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean.

Which explains the odd-looking ship that set off on its easterly course in 2018. The craft, a Norwegian-built research vessel named Seabed Constructor, was leased to Ocean Infinity, a deep-sea exploration firm with offices in Europe, Canada, Australia, and the United States. The Malaysian government contracted the company on a no-find, no-fee basis to look for MH370—a mission that promised a reward of up to $70 million. Over several months, Ocean Infinity used its autonomous subs to scan a grid of 9,600 square miles just north of the location where the original underwater search took place. By May of that year, having found nothing, the company suspended its mission.

Bringing the story of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to a definitive close has been equal parts confounding and elusive. A fool’s errand, one might say. But in spring 2025, the government of Malaysia again contracted the firm—now equipped with new vessels of its own design, as well as advanced underwater robots—to mount a fresh search for MH370. In taking up the search again, in one of the toughest marine environments in the world, Ocean Infinity would be risking money and its reputation in the process. What if, for the second time, it failed to find a debris field of MH370 under the waters of the southern Indian Ocean? What if the black boxes couldn’t be located? What if we never get a definitive answer to how Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 went missing without a trace?

After its 12:42 a.m. takeoff from Kuala Lumpur, with 227 passengers and 10 flight attendants on board, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 quickly reached its cruising altitude of 35,000 feet and steered toward Beijing. Flying the plane were first officer Fariq Abdul Hamid, 27, and pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah, 53. For Hamid, this was his final training flight before becoming a fully certified pilot. He was in good hands. Zaharie (who was known by his first name) was one of the most senior captains at Malaysia Airlines. He also owned a sophisticated Microsoft flight simulator that he used frequently at home.

At 1:08 a.m., MH370 flew out over the Malaysian coastline, soaring above the South China Sea toward Vietnam. Just 11 minutes later, when the handoff from Kuala Lumpur controllers to Vietnam’s air traffic jurisdiction was about to take place, air traffic control in Kuala Lumpur radioed MH370 one final time.

“Malaysian three-seven-zero, contact Ho Chi Minh one-two-zero-decimal-nine. Good night,” they said.

“Good night. Malaysian three-seven-zero,” came the reply from the cockpit.

Those were the last words ever heard from the plane.

Soon the Vietnamese controllers saw MH370 cross into its airspace. But then something unexpected happened. Air traffic relies on secondary radar, whereby a transponder on an airplane sends a signal that contains information identifying the plane and its cruising altitude. This flight, instead, disappeared entirely from air traffic radar at 1:21 a.m. It wasn’t until four hours later, at around 5:30 a.m., that any sort of emergency response commenced.

The simple fact was that at 6:30 a.m. on March 8, MH370—carrying passengers from China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand, France, Canada, the U.S., Ukraine, Russia, Iran, and the Netherlands—should have landed in Beijing. It didn’t.

Making sense of how an object as large as a Boeing 777 goes poof in the night is hard to fathom in our modern age. And for the human mind, which craves order and explanation, it is downright maddening—which might explain the bevy of individuals, with no connection to the flight whatsoever, who jumped in eager to provide answers. Over the many years since MH370’s disappearance, a variety of theories emerged about what happened to the plane. One scenario involves MH370 traveling toward Diego Garcia, a small atoll in the Indian Ocean where the U.S. has an army base, before being shot down. Another scenario claims the plane landed in the jungles of Cambodia. Other theories as to what happened to the flight received major airtime in 2023 during Netflix’s three-part docuseries MH370: The Plane That Disappeared. The plane, one person speculated, was hijacked by Russian agents and rerouted to Kazakhstan. Another person claimed the U.S. Air Force shot down MH370 over the South China Sea.

Whether the U.S. Air Force was really responsible was never seriously considered by Malaysia. But officials had suspected that the plane crashed in the South China Sea en route to Beijing. Accident investigators from Europe, Australia, and the U.S. teamed up with the Malaysian government and began searching the sea’s surface for any floating debris. That search was called off in April 2014 when nothing was found.

Yet within a week after MH370 apparently flew off the map, another theory surfaced in the Wall Street Journal. The article contains, to this day, the most plausible and reasonable explanation, one agreed upon by experts in aviation, satellite communications, and government: MH370 continued flying for hours after it disappeared from radar, turned west, away from its expected destination in Beijing, and then southward, ultimately meeting its demise in the waters of the southern Indian Ocean.

After the article was published, the Malaysian government eventually admitted that the account was true—which meant it had carried on a pointless search in the South China Sea for weeks. (In a comprehensive article for The Atlantic written in 2019, the late author and pilot William Langewiesche noted that autocratic bureaucracies with government-owned airlines generally want bad press to go away. It would be better, in other words, not to solve the puzzle, but to make the matter fade into memory as quickly as possible.)

To arrive at such a conclusion, the WSJ relied on an analysis of technical data from Inmarsat, a company that provides satellite services on land, at sea, and in the air. Although MH370 disappeared from air traffic radar screens, a feat easily achieved by whomever was manning the cockpit controls, it continued to link up every so often to a geostationary Inmarsat satellite over the Indian Ocean. Called “handshakes,” these linkups are electronic blips that, while tiny, yielded the most information about what happened to the plane. There were seven handshakes altogether: two that came automatically from the plane, and five others initiated automatically from an Inmarsat ground station in Perth, Australia.

The Inmarsat linkups provided two critical values. The first value is the burst timing offset, or BTO. It’s a measure of the round-trip time it takes for a blip to go from a ground station to a satellite to (in this case) an aircraft, then back up to the satellite and back to the ground station. It’s essentially the distance between the plane and the satellite, and that information gets processed as a series of rings, or arcs, of all possible locations. When it comes to MH370, the most important arc is the last one, the seventh, which the plane crossed at 8:19 a.m. Kuala Lumpur time. What’s important to note is that the seventh arc contains two location possibilities: If MH370 turned north, it may have ended up in Kazakhstan. If it went south, its location is in the southern Indian Ocean.

Determining the direction comes down to the second value: burst frequency offset, or BFO. It shows the difference between the expected frequency from a transmitter and the frequency ultimately received. As Langewiesche explained, the BFO is “a measure of radio-frequency Doppler shifts associated with high-speed movement in relation to satellite position.” Think about it and it makes sense: Neither planes nor satellites are stationary objects, so expected signals won’t match signals that actually get transmitted between the two. (That’s the Doppler effect, that change in frequency of radio waves.) Measuring BFO is a way to determine a plane’s speed and heading. During their investigation into the satellite data, Inmarsat technicians in London picked up on a distortion in the BFO value that suggested MH370 turned south at 2:40 a.m. Further analysis showed that MH370 entered a steep descent, as much as 15,000 feet per minute, just before crossing the seventh arc, which presumably happened after the plane ran out of fuel and both of its engines failed. From there it would have plunged violently into the ocean and shattered into millions of confetti-like pieces, to use Langewiesche’s analogy.

And it’s the satellite data, too, that paints a picture of MH370’s deviated flight path. Once the plane disappeared from secondary radar, it did an about-face over the South China Sea, flew back across Malaysia, over the Strait of Malacca separating Malaysia to the northeast and Indonesia to the southwest, and then, very suddenly, made a sharp turn to the southwest, away from the Andaman Sea to the west of Thailand. Accident investigators later determined that this turn was so tight there was no way the plane was still operating on autopilot. Someone was actively steering it.

What the satellite data doesn’t explain is why this happened—or who might have been flying the plane. Was it a potential hijacker? The available evidence says no: Malaysian and Chinese investigators, aided by American FBI agents, ran background checks on all passengers and flight attendants and cleared them of suspicion.

That left the pilots. Fariq Abdul Hamid was a young man with a fresh career as a prestigious Malaysia Airlines pilot ahead of him. Meanwhile, pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah was portrayed in official reports as “someone beyond reproach.” Just a simple family man. Yet as Langewiesche discovered during his reporting in Malaysia, the official depiction of Zaharie did not align with the man’s private life: His wife had moved out, and he was “often lonely and sad.” He admitted to his own friends that he spent his off-hours “pacing empty rooms waiting for the days between flights to go by.” Among aviation investigators, there was strong suspicion, Langewiesche wrote, that Zaharie was clinically depressed.

And then there’s his flight simulator. Most times, Zaharie let simulated flights play out, from wheels up to wheels down. But a forensic investigation of his simulator showed that Zaharie had done a dry run of a flight profile that eerily mirrored MH370’s final flight path. What’s more, Langewiesche reported, “he advanced the flight manually in multiple stages, repeatedly jumping the flight forward and subtracting the fuel as necessary until it was gone.”

Was it Zaharie? One of the pilot’s lifelong friends, another Boeing 777 captain, told Langewiesche he believed it could have been. It’s not like such an event is without precedent: In 1999, for example, the copilot of EgyptAir Flight 990 intentionally crashed the plane into the ocean just south of Nantucket, Massachusetts. In 2015, the copilot of a Germanwings airliner deliberately crashed that plane into the French Alps. In a report published in 2014, the Federal Aviation Administration cites eight different examples of pilot suicides. And surveys conducted of pilots show that 4 percent have thought about taking their own lives.

As the search pressed on over the years, a group of researchers called the Independent Group emerged, made up of engineers and satellite experts who had found one another online as they simultaneously researched the MH370 crash. One of them, an engineer from Virginia named Victor Iannello, was the person who analyzed Zaharie’s simulated flight, coming to the conclusion that the simulation wasn’t some random event, but rather a potentially pivotal clue as to what happened on MH370’s final flight.

“Until MH370 is found and the reason for its disappearance is known, we will be bombarded with conspiracy theories, false leads, books, and movies which will provide nothing but conjecture,” said Prahlad Shirsath three months after the crash. His wife, Kranti, had been on board. “We need to find the truth,” he continued, “and ensure this never happens again.”

Where is that truth? Perhaps at the bottom of the Indian Ocean, the suspected location of the flight’s data recorder and cockpit voice recorder. Recovering the black boxes might help investigators resolve what happened to MH370. But we have to find them first.

The ocean is vast, and the ocean is scary. The deep ocean especially. Consider, for a moment, the possibility that we know more about Earth’s immediate orbit than we know about its oceans. In space, more than 9,000 satellites roam. On Earth, barely one-quarter of the planet’s oceans are mapped in any coherent way so as to make them discernible for underwater exploration.

In May 2014, the governments of Malaysia and China agreed that the Australians should lead the search for MH370, under the auspices of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau. Fugro, a Dutch firm, was contracted to do the work, with payment coming from Malaysia, China, and Australia. Given the satellite data that suggested splashdown on or about the seventh arc, an area of roughly 11,500 square miles across the arc was selected for exploration. This put the search area between 930 and 1,700 miles away from Australia’s western coast.

“Unforgivable” is perhaps the best word for describing the conditions of the Indian Ocean where search efforts were concentrated. The area saw ripping winds as high as 50 miles an hour, sudden powerful storms marked by 30-foot-high swells, and dense rain and fog. These were the least ideal conditions for sending ships out to sea for long periods of time, far from the closest ports, in a search for the maritime equivalent of a needle in a haystack.

When the underwater search for the remains of MH370 finally kicked off, the depths of the southern Indian Ocean were a mystery. An impressive level of surveying was conducted between May and December of 2014—with further mapping through early 2017—to even understand the topography of the deep ocean floor in this part of the world. It had never been mapped before. Fugro deployed three ships: the Equator, equipped with a hull-mounted echo sounder (to measure depth); the Discovery, with side-scan sonar; and the Supporter, which deployed a single autonomous underwater vehicle with side scanners, sonar, and an echo sounder. In all, close to 275,000 square miles of the deep ocean was surveyed, an area much larger than the search zone but valuable nonetheless for understanding the terrain.

Ridges, peaks, valleys, even underwater volcanoes covered the seabed. Most concerning was a deep underwater canyon that sliced horizontally through the seventh arc, believed by some to be the area where the remains of MH370 would be found. Dubbed Broken Ridge, it was formed by tectonic plate shifts more than 40 million years ago. Its depths reached between 2,000 and 20,000 feet beneath the ocean’s surface; sections of its topography were covered in sediment as thick as 1,000 feet.

“It’s like trying to imagine the Rocky Mountains underwater,” says Mike Exner, another member of the Independent Group. Exner is a retired entrepreneur from Colorado with a background in electrical engineering and satellite communications, having founded several of his own companies. He has also been a licensed pilot for more than 50 years. Exner was the person who studied Inmarsat data and civilian radar—primary radar scans resulting from simple pings about objects in the sky—to conclude that in MH370’s final hours, a flight to the seventh arc would not have been possible if there had been some sort of computer glitch or other systems failure.

“All those turns had to be done manually,” Exner says. “I think we’re about 99 percent sure Zaharie did it.” He adds that he can’t be 100 percent sure but says that once you consider the backgrounds of his copilot, the cabin crew, and the passengers, many of the signs point to him.

For almost three years, Fugro’s ships looked across areas on or near the seventh arc for any signs of the plane. Admittedly, there was a technological element working against them. Autonomous underwater vehicles have been game changers in underwater search and rescue, but they still come with certain drawbacks. Traditional radio waves with meaningful data rates don’t penetrate seawater at even paltry depths of six inches. Communication from ship or shore to a vehicle relies instead on sound waves. But even those become useless once the vehicle is roughly five miles away from its launch point.

“You have more contact with the Mars rover than you do [with] . . . a deep survey vehicle,” says J. Carl Hartsfield, director and senior program manager of the Oceanographic Systems Lab at the nonprofit Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts.

So we humans have to place a great deal of trust in technology that we can’t control once it gets out into the ocean. What’s more, Fugro had only one autonomous underwater vehicle at its disposal, and its maximum diving depth was 13,000 feet, which meant it wasn’t reaching the seabed most of the time. As the years went on, the search zone was expanded from the original 23,000 square miles to an area surpassing 46,000 square miles. But not a scrap of the plane was found, and on January 17, 2017, the Australian-led search was suspended, pending further evidence of the plane’s location.

Could it be that MH370 really isn’t near the seventh arc? Could it have ended up somewhere else? David Mearns, a marine scientist who has led several deep-ocean explorations, says there are only two ways to explain why any piece of the aircraft wasn’t found underwater.

“One, they haven’t looked in the right place. Or two, they’ve looked in the right place, but they missed it,” he says. “Anybody who comes up with anything else doesn’t know what they’re talking about.”

By the time Ocean Infinity arrived at the scene of the crash in January 2018, much more had been deduced about MH370’s probable location. While the initial underwater search took place, an amateur campaign to search for debris from the missing plane began. At the center of this was Blaine Gibson, a Seattle-based lawyer with a penchant for wearing a fedora. (The connection to Indiana Jones isn’t lost on him. By his own admission, Gibson is fascinated by mysteries and archaeology. According to him, he once went searching for the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-plated chest containing the tablets on which the Ten Commandments were inscribed.)

“I was astonished to learn that there was no organized search of beaches and shorelines,” he says. “It always seemed to me that the first piece of debris from this plane was probably just going to be found washed to shore by someone walking on the beach.”

He was right. In July 2015, a flaperon, an airfoil that attaches to a plane wing next to the flap, was discovered by a beach cleaning crew on the French island of Réunion, more than 3,500 miles west of Australia. A right wing flap was found on Pemba Island off the coast of Tanzania, in East Africa, in June 2016. And about four months earlier that same year, Gibson located a honeycomb object broken off from a plane’s horizontal stabilizer with the words “No Step” written on it, a piece that was confirmed to be “almost certainly from MH370 by matching part number, stencil, paint, and composition,” says Gibson. In all, more than 50 pieces of debris have been found so far, much of it on Africa’s eastern coast. (The currents in the Southern Hemisphere move in a counterclockwise swirl: east to west when they’re close to the equator; the opposite direction farther south.)

The significance of the physical evidence can’t be overstated. It appears to confirm that the plane crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, that it shattered on impact, and that there should still be more debris left on the ocean floor. The discoveries also refined the search area: Drift analysis conducted by the University of Western Australia put the crash site at a latitude somewhere between 28.3 degrees south and 33.2 degrees south.

In other words, the evidence provided Ocean Infinity a tighter target. In 2018, Seabed Constructor started its search grid at about 35 degrees south and some 1,300 miles to the southwest of Australia’s west coast. It was also better equipped this time, having brought eight autonomous free-swimming submersibles called HUGINs. These robot crafts, designed and manufactured by Norway-based Kongsberg Discovery, are able to reach depths of 20,000 feet. Each comes with a lithium-polymer battery pack weighing 660 pounds; that allows for around 60 hours of uninterrupted search time. Each is also equipped with a downward-pointing sonar system as well as side-mounted sonars to send out pings to objects on the ocean floor. Onboard magnetometers on every HUGIN can confirm whether a return ping indicates something metallic in nature.

Back in January 2018, The Economist reported that Seabed Constructor was “the most advanced civilian survey vessel,” and predicted that if it couldn’t find MH370, it was “likely that nothing will, and that the mystery of MH370 will remain unsolved.” In May, Ocean Infinity turned back to port, having found nothing on the ocean floor.

That two underwater searches proved fruitless has led to differing views as to where, exactly, the plane landed in the southern Indian Ocean. Richard Godfrey, a retired British aerospace engineer and a founding member of the Independent Group, believes the plane is farther north on the seventh arc. His conclusion largely rests on an analysis he’s conducted of data from WSPR, or Weak Signal Propagation Reporter. Amateur radio operators constantly send test signals and record the data that comes back. Godfrey says that when an aircraft flies through such a signal, it creates a disruption that can be used to track that craft. His results put MH370 inside an 18-mile circle at 29.128 degrees south latitude, approximately 970 miles west of Perth.

“It will only take one more search of this area,” Godfrey told the BBC in 2024, “and we will find MH370.”

Meanwhile, other research groups think differently. One contends MH370 is farther east of the seventh arc, in a 20,000-foot-deep hole that lies along the longitudinal line of Penang Island just off Malaysia’s western coast. Two separate groups believe that MH370 did not dive into the ocean and shatter; they think MH370 came to a controlled, guided landing, and then sank. Part of their argument rests on anomalies in the BFO data, those radio-frequency Doppler shifts. The predicted BFO came in at a much higher frequency than what was observed, possibly indicating that initial thoughts of where the aircraft came to rest are wrong.

One of those pushing this interpretation is Vincent Lyne, a former researcher at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania. He laid out his argument in a paper published in December 2024 and called special attention to the two large-scale searches along the seventh arc.

“A significant positive outcome for ocean research was the huge volume of seafloor data collected across [about 46,000 square miles],” he wrote. “It still remains the most intensely mapped seafloor area of our planet. MH370 was simply not there!”

How these interpretations factored into Ocean Infinity’s new search was unclear. The company is tight-lipped and declined an interview for this article, but CEO Oliver Plunkett did acknowledge Godfrey’s WSPR research in a 2022 teleconference with relatives who lost people on Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

If there’s a new dispute over the fate of MH370, it rests largely on where the plane will be found in the southern Indian Ocean, and not that the plane is somewhere under the seas in that part of the world. Gibson, who discovered part of the plane’s horizontal stabilizer, maintains that there’s no way a controlled landing took place. He cites the more than 50 pieces of debris that have been recovered since MH370 went down. “It’s not intact under water,” he tells me.

Exner, for his part, thinks the WSPR data is no substitute for the Inmarsat satellite communications. “Focus strictly on the seventh arc between 32 and 36 degrees south latitude,” he says. “[MH370 is] probably within 50 miles of that arc. Even though [Ocean Infinity] didn’t find it in the first search, that doesn’t mean it isn’t there.”

When Ocean Infinity ultimately resumed its quest for MH370, it was going back with even newer technology. In the time since its 2018 search, the company had built a fleet of more than 15 ships, ranging from vessels as short as 46 feet and as long as 282 feet. While small crews could climb aboard these ships, all of the vessels were nonetheless designed for remote operation from Ocean Infinity’s control centers at company locations. Ocean Infinity had also developed a line of proprietary underwater autonomous vehicles and acquired additional HUGIN submersibles to aid in its efforts.

The company had also accrued a solid track record of successful searches. Just under six months after Ocean Infinity suspended its search for MH370 in 2018, it discovered the lost Argentine Navy submarine San Juan in the Atlantic Ocean. The following year, it located the remains of the South Korean supertanker Stellar Daisy, which sank in the South Atlantic in 2017. In 2024, Ocean Infinity discovered the wreck of a U.S. World War II destroyer, USS Stewart, that the U.S. Navy had sunk deliberately for target practice in the waters of the Pacific Ocean off San Francisco.

Despite all that, Ocean Infinity trawled the unforgiving waters of the southern Indian Ocean for a few days in March 2025 until rough seas forced it back to port. It resumed searching in late December 2025 and kept at it through January 23, 2026, before departing the search area empty-handed.

“The scale of the challenge both geographically and technologically is almost impossible to comprehend,” said Ocean Infinity’s Plunkett in a March 2026 press release. “If nothing else, we can say with confidence that it isn’t where we looked. That matters—it brings clarity, and it will help those continuing to study the evidence refine their thinking and shape future search strategies.”

Underwater searches, obviously, are not easy or cheap endeavors. When Air France Flight 447 bound for Paris from Rio de Janeiro crashed and sank in the Atlantic Ocean off the northeastern coast of Brazil in 2009, the search team that was dispatched knew where to look for the Airbus jet. And despite it resting at a depth of only about 13,000 feet, the searchers still took almost two years to find it.

Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution’s Hartsfield, whose lab helped facilitate that search, can’t remember the exact figures but estimates that the ships deployed in the search operate at a cost of around $65,000 a day. The Remus 6000 Autonomous Underwater Vehicle used to locate the Airbus cost about another $15,000 a day (in 2026 dollars).

“Although this phase of the search has concluded, our commitment has not,” said Plunkett. “We’re continuing to work with the Malaysian government in the hope of being able to return when circumstances allow.” Ocean Infinity’s current contract runs until June 2026, which means if it hasn’t happened, it’s unlikely that a new search will get underway this year.

But as technology continues to advance, maybe someday an armada of vessels will hit the rough seas near the seventh arc once again—probing the depths, scanning the seabed, sending sonar scans into the darkness—and unearth the newest blips of hope in this maddening unsolved mystery.

Andrew Zaleski, a writer based near Washington, D.C., covers science, technology, and business.

#6549. What Could Split a Black Hole in Two?

We all know that black holes can collide. It has happened since black holes began to form, early in cosmic time. The result is always a clash that gives off gravitational waves and a giant bang. Since black holes have such strong gravity, it's almost impossible to imagine a way that any force could break one apart. Yet, that's the task that a group of scientists in Europe set for themselves.

In a study of possible mechanisms for black hole fragmentation, Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark, along with Giacomo Cacciapaglia (Laboratoire de Physique ThÃ©orique et Hautes Ãnergies) and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center, conducted a series of calculations showing that under the right conditions, a black hole could split up into two black holes. It's an unusual possibility, to say the least, but the team has calculated what needs to happen if such an event were to occur.

The two pieces would have to stay apart, according to Sannino. "The two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," he said. If such a split-up could happen, the event horizon of the black hole would form a trouser-like shape as the split-up proceeded. Essentially, it would form two legs of a pair of pants, which is why the team called it a "pair-of-pants topology."

That's one possibility for what happens if/when a black hole splits into pieces. No one has seen such an event (yet), so it's still largely theoretical. There's one major impediment, however. That's called entropy, the measure of how many different microscopic ways a physical system can be arranged while still appearing the same from the outside. For example, a rock's shape can remain solid and static until some outside force changes it, such as heating. In the case of an ordinary, non-rotating black hole, breaking it into two pieces would reduce its entropy and make the process thermodynamically unlikely.

The black hole at the centre of M87. It has a measured spin, so theoretically, if conditions were right, it could break apart, according to a new study. Credit: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration

However, let's say we have a rotating black hole, spinning very rapidly. According to the team, such a system could break up into two pieces. However, they have to separate quickly, or risk falling back together. So, it turns out it could happen if both black holes have to keep rotating as fast as they possibly can (or close to it). But what would cause the split to occur? The answer lies in the rotation. It alters the relationship between black hole mass, its angular momentum as it spins, and entropy. It's possible that change could lead to the black hole fragmenting. If so, then the next steps are for the black hole "twins" to move apart and retain the momentum and speed of the original.

Focusing just on black holes, it seems pretty unlikely that such events have happened, but they don't want to say it's never happened. According to Sannino, the possibility is there, but in specific cases. "We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einsteinâs theory, and we are working to quantify this," he explained. "We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers."

When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

#6545. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

#6544. Hera Probe Sees Asteroid Pair Separately for First Time

Planetary defense is a growing concern among the scientific community, as efforts have been made to design and implement missions meant to deflect incoming threats to the Earth well in advance. In 2022, NASA intentionally collided the Double Asteroid Redirection test (DART) planetary defense spacecraft into the smaller asteroid of the binary asteroid, Didymos and Dimorphos, with the latter being the smaller one. While the goal was to ascertain if deflecting an asteroid is feasible, how did this influence the geological characteristics of Dimorphos, and what can it teach us about planetary defense missions?

This is the task of a brave robotic explorer known as Hera, which is a spacecraft mission led by the European Space Agency (ESA) in cooperation with NASA and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Hera recently sent back its first image of Didymos and Dimorphos, which orbit each other as they orbit the Sun, with the image revealing the two asteroids separated, as opposed to seeing a single dot. This comes after Hera was launched in October 2024 and is now about 1,280 kilometers (795 miles) from the well-known binary asteroid, the latter of which is about 197 million kilometers (122 million miles) from Earth. While the larger Didymos is estimated to be 780 meters (2,559 feet) in diameter, the much smaller Dimorphos is estimated to be about 151 meters (495 feet) across.

âFor the very first time we are seeing through Heraâs own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for,â said Ian Carnelli, who is the ESA Head of the Systems Department and the Hera mission manager. âOur views will much grow sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos â the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action â on 25 November [2026].â

As noted, the goal of the Hera mission will be to conduct follow-up observations and data collection for NASAâs DART planetary defense mission. For this mission, the DART spacecraft intentionally impacted Dimorphos with the goal of ascertaining whether impacting an object could deflect it away from impacting Earth. The intentional impact occurred in September 2022 at 6.1 km/s (3.8 mi/s), resulting in not only slowing Dimorphosâ orbit around Didymos by 32 to 33 minutes, with the initial goal being at least 73 seconds. Thus, the mission was deemed a resounding success, and the researchers even observed an ejecta plume from the surface of Dimorphos as far as 10,000 kilometers (6,214 miles) into space.

Aristic rendering of Hera approaching Dimorphos. (Credit: ESA-Science Office)

Along with conducting observational analyses of the post-collision Dimorphos surface, Hera will also deploy two shoebox-sixed CubeSats named Milani and Juventas since Hera canât fly that close to the surface. While Milaniâs task is to perform a close-up mineralogical analysis of the DART impact site, Juventas will be tasked with using ground-penetrating radar to peer about 100 meters (328 feet) beneath Dimorphosâ surface to ascertain whether its interior is solid rock or a loose rubble pile which has been proposed by researchers.

As noted, planetary defense is rapidly becoming a growing concern among not only the scientific community, but governments worldwide. This is primarily driven by our growing awareness of the number of asteroids in our solar system that cross Earthâs orbital path, but also the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor that blew out windows and injured more than 1,500 people, primarily from broken glass. But with this concern comes how to address, and a combination of NASAâs DART and Hera missions are providing key insights into how to deflect potential asteroid impactors that could cause widespread death and destruction if one impacts Earth.

What new insights into Didymos and Dimorphos will Hera and other space missions make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6542. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

#6541. Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI

NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972. But the famed agency has no intention of stopping there, as they plan to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon through a slow and meticulous process involving power, resource extraction, and habitat technologies. However, with the soaring use of artificial intelligence (AI) in our everyday lives, how could this emerging technology be used to identify new landing sites for future outposts on the Moon and possibly Mars?

Now, a team of researchers from The Ohio State University might have contributed to how AI can be used for future space outposts. As discussed in a recent study presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS 58) of the American Astronomical Society, the researchers introduced how a novel AI model could be used to both identify safe landing sites and develop a human outpost strategy at those landing sites. The model is called LUMINA, which is an agentic AI framework designed to help mission planners evaluate safe landing sites on the lunar surface, specifically focusing on key resources like water ice, along with potential scientific value.

To identify prime landing sites, LUMINA doesnât just rely on orbital images. It incorporates a myriad of lunar surface data, including topography and terrain hazards, scientific value, geology, surface properties, and even comparing the candidate landing sites to each other. As a result, LUMINA demonstrates a keen ability to identify landing sites across the lunar surface that could maximize mission success and effectiveness for both human habitation and science. But the researchers donât want to limit LUMINA to the Moon, as they envision LUMINA contributing to other planetary bodies, specifically Mars.

âAI systems are going to become critical tools for space exploration that will help humans analyze the millions of images and datasets that future missions will require,â said Gokce Inal, who is a PhD candidate in Civil Environmental and Geodetic Engineering at The Ohio State University and lead author of the study. âThis work is meant to serve as a bridge between those two worlds, AI and planetary science.â

LUMINA is built upon previous research by this same group called the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Lunar Exploration (LLaVA-LE), which demonstrated its ability to analyze and describe orbital images of the lunar surface. The LLaVA-LE model is currently available on arXiv, was recently presented at the CVPR2026 AI4Space Workshop in June 2026 and can be found on GitHub.

As noted, NASA has ambitious plans to establish a permanent human presence on the lunar surface with the long-term goal of sending humans to Mars. Developing the necessary technologies to accomplish both goals is part of NASAâs Moon to Mars Architecture, which is a constantly evolving strategic framework designed to develop and test vital technologies that will allow humans to work and live on the Moon that can then be used for human missions to the Red Planet. These technologies include power systems, transportation, habitation & life support, robotics & construction, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), communications, and more. The question then becomes how can AI, and specifically the LUMINA model, be used to further develop these technologies?

âNASAâs Artemis program creates important opportunities for our research,â said Inal. âAs new lunar data becomes available, their results can improve systems like ours and better support future mission planning.â

Of the technologies listed above, ISRU plays a crucial role in using local and available resources for crew use and survival. This includes water ice for drinking, bathing, fuel, and even oxygen from electrolysis, and using the lunar regolith to potentially grow plants and for construction. Also known as âliving off the landâ, ISRU aims to reduce, and potentially eliminate, the need for resupplies from Earth. Essentially, it wants to create a self-sustaining system exactly like life on Earth.

How will LUMINA help plan future space outposts on the Moon and Mars in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.

The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.

In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.

More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."

"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."

Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."

Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

#6539. Spiced and Glazed Roast Turkey

Our mission: A roast turkey that’s boldly spiced, beautifully glazed, and—can we type this loudly enough?—PROPERLY COOKED. That means juicy breast meat, tender dark meat, and plenty of deeply browned skin. Andy Baraghani and Brad Leone’s solution? Break the bird into five pieces: two wings, two legs, and one whole breast. Roasting the bird in parts gives you more control over when each piece is done—no dry breast meat or tough legs.

They didn’t slouch on flavor either. A peppery dry brine with garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika gets to work 24–48 hours before the turkey goes into the oven. Then comes the glaze: a savory-tangy mix of soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, orange zest, and herbs. Brushed onto the turkey as it roasts, it builds a glossy, deeply burnished finish. And because the pieces cook on a wire rack set inside a baking sheet, you get more exposed skin for browning and a more even cook overall.

If the idea of doing surgery on a raw turkey gives you a stress rash, ask your butcher to do it—even at the supermarket. Request a 12–14-lb. turkey cut into five pieces, with the thighs attached to the drumsticks, the breast left whole, and the backbone removed. If they ask why, just say: Yes, you’re making that ridiculous Bon Appétit recipe. If you’d rather do the honors yourself, here’s our guide to breaking down a whole turkey.

Choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. Many supermarket birds are already treated with a salt solution, sometimes labeled “self-basting,” “enhanced,” or “contains a solution.” Adding this dry brine on top can make the turkey overly salty. Check the packaging before you buy.

Should I rinse off the dry brine before roasting?

No. Leave the seasoning on the turkey when you coat it with oil. Some of the spice mixture may rub off, but that’s fine. There’s no need to rinse the bird, and washing raw poultry can spread bacteria around your kitchen.

Can I use the pan drippings to make gravy?

Yes, but taste them first. Between the seasoned dry brine and soy-based glaze, the drippings can be quite salty and intensely flavored. Use them sparingly and taste your gravy before adding more salt. For a simpler option, try our Make-Ahead Gravy, which doesn’t require drippings at all.

Read our guide to turkey cooking times, no matter the bird’s size or your preferred cooking method.

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 24 hours dry-brining

Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck and giblets removed, breast side up, on a cutting board and pat dry. Grip a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate the wing from the breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get into the place where the joint meets the socket). Remove wing; repeat on the other side.

Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until the ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through the joint to separate leg. Repeat on the other side.

Now for the breast: Position the turkey breast side down with the opening facing you. Using kitchen shears, cut along one side of backbone until you get all the way through the neck end, then turn the turkey 180° and cut through the other side to remove the backbone (save it for making stock).

Very finely grind 2 Tbsp. whole black peppercorns and 2 Tbsp. whole pink or black peppercorns in a spice mill or mortar and pestle; transfer to a medium bowl. Add ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. garlic powder, 2 Tbsp. onion powder, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1 Tbsp. smoked paprika, and use your fingers to mix together.

Place turkey pieces, skin side up, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. Sprinkle salt mixture liberally all over turkey, patting to adhere. You may not need all of it, but it’s good to have extra since some will end up on the baking sheet. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 24 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil to make cleanup easy and set rack back inside. Arrange turkey pieces on rack, skin side up, and let sit at room temperature up to 2 hours to help decrease the cooking time.

Meanwhile, cook small handful of hardy herbs (such as sage, rosemary, bay leaves, and/or thyme), 4 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, ⅓ cup low-sodium soy sauce, ⅓ cup (packed; 71 g) light brown sugar, and ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until sugar is dissolved and glaze thickens slightly (it should just barely coat a spoon), 10–12 minutes. Remove glaze from heat.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Rub turkey with 6 Tbsp. neutral oil (such as vegetable, peanut, or canola) and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet. Roast turkey, rotating baking sheet halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown, 20–25 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 20 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast registers 150°, and 170° when inserted into the thickest part of the thighs, 50–70 minutes longer (total cooking time will be 1–1½ hours). Skin should be deep golden brown and shiny. Transfer turkey to a cutting board; tent loosely with foil. Let rest 30–60 minutes before carving.

Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published in our November 2019 issue. We’ve updated the introduction with additional cooking guidance and answers to common reader questions; we’ve also updated the recipe for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving recipes →

#6537. Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits

The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an âasteroidâ since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceresâ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceresâ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several âbright spotsâ, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceresâ formation and evolution?

Now, a pair of researchers from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) might have inched our way to better understanding a connection between Ceresâ water ice activity and surface salt deposits. As discussed in findings published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets (JGR: Planets), the researcher presented evidence that past data might have been incorrect regarding the amount of salt deposits previously observed by NASAâs Dawn spacecraft, which explored Ceres from 2015 to 2018.

For the study, researchers used a combination of Dawn spacecraft data and a series of computer models to examine the evolution of surface water ice and salt deposits on Ceresâ surface. The primary motivation behind the study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding observational results of surface water ice and salt deposits versus whatâs actually happening. Specifically, this study focused on the transition of water ice to salt deposits through evaporation (scientifically called sublimation) and whether data collected from Dawn accurately estimated the amount of water ice and salt.

In the end, the researchers found that the salt deposits might be hidden by the water ice deposits theyâre mixed with, with the salt deposits potentially existing in larger amounts than previously hypothesized, estimated to be between 30 to 50 percent greater. Additionally, they found that landslides (scientifically called mass wasting) contribute to more surface ice being exposed, which then evaporate, leaving behind the salty bright spots observed by Dawn. They note some water ice deposits could have been observed by Dawn that could have been recently exposed from landslides.

âWe proposed a qualitative model of long-term surface evolution of Ceres' salty ices based on observations that is akin to thermal segregation [sorting] on icy satellites,â the study notes. âIce in deposits with salts sublimates more readily and may move to colder areas, resulting in a feedback that creates compositional differences between colder, icy surfaces and warmer, salt-richer regions. Ongoing replenishment of ice at the optical [visible] surface is required to reconcile multiple detections with geologically negligible lifetimes of ice. The finding resolves an existing paradox about how salt-rich deposits arise in the Ceres near-surface; they are likely not initially salt-rich but instead result from enrichment of salt at the optical surface by sublimation of salty ices.â

Essentially, the salt-water ice deposits are sorted based on heat and evaporation, the salt within water ice mixture causes the water ice to evaporate faster, leaving behind the salt deposits. This creates a feedback loop that results in different mixture amounts and types among separate water ice and salt deposits. Additionally, the surface water ice is exposed from landslides, adding to this evaporation feedback loop. Finally, the study fills a longstanding misunderstanding between how salt deposits are formed and evolve, in that they donât start out with heavy amounts of salt. Instead, they start out with low amounts of salt but have their salt contents increase from the evaporation of water ice that also contains salt.

What new insights into Ceresâ salt deposits and water ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6536. I’m So Obsessed With This Coffee Mug, I Tell Strangers About It

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.
