The outer solar system will descend into chaos just a few billion years after the sun exhausts its fuel ‪—‬ much sooner than scientists previously thought, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the sun inevitably dies, not even the outer solar system will be safe from the resulting chaos, new research hints.Scientists have long thought the outer solar system ‪—‬ which comprises the four giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — would mostly retain its present-day appearance for hundreds of billions of years to come. But a new study suggests that the outer giants may develop weirdly shaped orbits as the sun runs out of fuel, causing the planets to cross paths and destroy themselves through collisions within three billion years of the sun's transformation into a red giant.

The findings, published Sept. 21 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could change our understanding of what kinds of exoplanets orbit certain stars.

In about 5 billion years, the sun will balloon outward as a red giant after exhausting all of the hydrogen in its core. During this red giant phase, our star will swell to 100 times its present-day size, gobbling up Mercury, Venus and possibly even Earth in the process, Nathan Kaib, a planetary scientist at the University of Oklahoma who wasn't involved in the new research, told Live Science in an email. Following this violent swelling, the sun will crumple into a collapsed core called a white dwarf.

Until now, scientists thought the four outer planets would escape this phase relatively unscathed. A 1998 simulation-based study suggested that the gas the sun spews from its outer layers will push this planetary quartet outward, doubling the radius of each planet's orbit. Only the gravitational impact of a runaway star could destabilize this new order, and such events are thought to occur only once every billion billion years.

These predictions hinged on the assumption that the sun will eject its outer layers smoothly. However, recent observations of stars suggest a jerkier loss of mass, with gas clouds lofted by plumes of plasma in the sun — as though our star were spitting out mass blobs. "They're kind of like coronal mass ejections, except much larger," Jim Fuller, a professor of theoretical astrophysics at Caltech and co-author of the new study, told Live Science in an email.

Each "blob" pushes the star backward, similar to how a fired bullet causes a gun to recoil. Although every push is small, moving the sun just a few feet per second, many pushes can, over time, impart the equivalent of an enormous kick that alters the sun's speed by several hundred feet per second. In fact, astronomers have already seen white dwarfs suffer such kicks in other star systems.

An illustration of the sun releasing a giant mass of plasma. As such large explosions increase in the sun's dying days, the recoil could disrupt the gravitational balance of the outer solar system.

When Fuller, who studied these kicks, described them to Konstantin Batygin, a professor of planetary science at Caltech and the study's first author, Batygin "realized this would have important consequences for the evolution of our own solar system," Fuller said. That's because the kicks change the sun's gravitational pulls on everything around it.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To determine how the sun's mass loss would influence the giant planets, Batygin created computer-based simulations of the sun and the outer planets. The researchers considered three scenarios: if the sun lost its mass smoothly, if it spit out distinct mass blobs during its entire time evolving as a red giant, and if the sun spewed the blobs only during its last stages. The researchers also varied each ejected blob's mass.

The first scenario produced results similar to those of previous studies, with the outer solar system retaining almost all of its features for billions of years. In contrast, the other two cases had drastically different results. Using 672 simulations, the researchers found that if the sun lost mass in blobs, the giant planets would be thrown into chaos, switching places, developing weirdly oval-shaped orbits, and even getting ejected out of the solar system entirely. Most dramatically, in 96% of the simulations with the heaviest ejected mass packets, the planets get destroyed as they crashed into each other.

These developments also happened much more rapidly — less than a few hundred million years after the sun transformed into a white dwarf, or even during the red giant phase, in the most extreme scenarios.

The study's findings hint that analogues of the present-day outer solar system around white dwarf stars are less likely to exist than previously thought. Kaib noted that the study's results suggest that planets with oval-shaped orbits should dominate instead. It's thought that habitable planets could exist around white dwarfs, but this study's findings show that our understanding of those distant star systems may be incomplete, and that such worlds may, in reality, be unstable.

Batygin, K., Fuller, J., & Adams, F. C. (2026). Terminal instability of the solar system triggered by stochastic solar mass loss. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1009(2), L22. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea290

#6533. Comets Probably Didn’t Bring Life’s Ingredients to Earth After All, New Study Reveals

New research suggests Mars may have been better suited than Earth to receive life’s chemical ingredients from comets, although the chances remain surprisingly slim.

Comets have long been considered possible sources of the chemical ingredients that helped life emerge on Earth. But new research suggests these icy visitors were extremely unlikely to deliver those molecules in sufficient quantities, challenging a theory that has shaped scientific thinking for nearly a century.

Using advanced computer simulations, researchers led by the University of Cambridge found that comet impacts would almost always destroy fragile organic compounds before they could contribute to the chemistry of early life. Even under favorable conditions, successful delivery would have been extraordinarily rare. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, also suggest that Mars may have offered slightly better conditions for receiving these molecules.

Comets contain carbon and nitrogen-bearing compounds, including hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule involved in chemical reactions that can produce some of life’s essential building blocks. Their ability to transport these substances across the Solar System has made them central to theories about how prebiotic chemistry began on Earth.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get out of jail free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The problem lies in the violence of comet impacts. According to the simulations, comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make the survival of their organic cargo extremely unlikely. Most of these molecules would vaporize during impact rather than reach the surface intact. The researchers reached this conclusion by combining models of comet trajectories, atmospheric interactions, impact physics, and the formation and evolution of comet populations.

To investigate the likelihood of successful delivery, the team concentrated on HCN, which is regularly detected in Solar System comets. Their calculations showed that impacts capable of preserving the molecule and depositing it at useful concentrations would have been exceptionally uncommon.

The number of comets striking Earth also fell sharply during the planet’s first 500 million years, leaving at most a handful of opportunities for meaningful HCN delivery. Even if some molecules survived, they would likely disperse before the chemical reactions needed for life’s emergence could advance far enough.

“It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going,” said Anslow. “We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”

The investigation builds on earlier research published in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues proposed that closely spaced planets could help comets deliver organic molecules. In such systems, gravitational encounters might allow comets to move between planets while gradually slowing down, increasing the chances that their chemical cargo could survive an eventual impact.

The new study examined whether similar conditions could have existed in our Solar System, using recent advances in simulations of comet impacts and planetary dynamics.

“We’re learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century,” Anslow said.

If comets were not a major source of Earth’s prebiotic molecules, other explanations remain possible. Asteroids struck the early Earth much more frequently, and their impacts could have triggered chemical reactions that produced organic compounds. Alternatively, the necessary ingredients may have formed through chemical processes occurring on Earth itself, without requiring delivery from space.

Although the results cast doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, the researchers identified Mars as a somewhat more favorable destination. Mars is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere, conditions that could allow more cometary material to reach its surface. This may have increased the chances of organic molecules surviving impacts during the Solar System’s early history, when comet collisions were more common.

However, the simulations do not establish that comets successfully delivered prebiotic molecules to Mars. They indicate only that the process may have been more feasible there than on Earth.

“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” said Anslow. “Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”

The findings could also help astronomers assess the chemical environments of planets orbiting other stars. In planetary systems where several worlds orbit close together, gravitational interactions might slow incoming comets enough to improve the prospects for delivering organic molecules.

Future observatories, including proposed successors to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory, could help investigate these planetary systems. Identifying environments where “bouncing” comets might survive long enough to deliver their chemical cargo could provide one way to narrow the search for potentially habitable worlds.

Reference: “Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth” by Richard J. Anslow, Catriona H. McDonald, Amy Bonsor, Paul B. Rimmer and Auriol S. P. Rae, 28 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y

The research was supported in part by the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

#6532. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6531. 120 Million Years Ago, Something Extraordinary Was Happening in Earth’s Oceans

Colombia’s ancient seas supported an extraordinary diversity of top predators, offering clues to how life may undergo major evolutionary changes without a mass extinction.

Mass extinctions have reshaped life on Earth, but they may not be the only way ecosystems undergo dramatic evolutionary change.

Roughly 120 million years ago, the seas covering what is now central Colombia were home to an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators. Fossils from this remarkably complex ecosystem suggest that some of evolution’s biggest turning points may unfold without a catastrophic mass extinction.

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) houses most of the formation’s fossils. The research at McGill University and CIP was conducted by PhD graduate Dirley Cortés and Professor Hans Larsson of McGill’s Department of Biology.

“This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others,” Cortés explained. “Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.”

In a previous study, the researchers estimated the Paja Biota’s food web, the network of feeding relationships among its animals. They found it was among the most complex ever to have evolved, with a high diversity of apex predators, animals at the top of the food chain.

“The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish,” Larsson said.

The researchers suspect that greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, and nutrient-rich coastal waters helped support this exceptional biodiversity and biological transition. New marine connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic oceans through what is now Colombia were probably also part of that rare convergence. Many of these same factors help drive biodiversity today, they noted.

Cortés and Larsson propose calling the pattern a “Biotic Inflection,” a period when many evolutionary lineages nearing extinction coexist with newly emerging groups that later diversify.

“I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said.

Testing the proposal will require additional fossil sampling, more precise dating, and comparisons with deposits elsewhere in the world. Those investigations would help establish how widespread the Biotic Inflection pattern was and when similar events may have occurred in Earth’s history.

Reference: “The Paja Formation of Colombia records uniquely high biodiversity during a biotic inflection in an Early Cretaceous Gondwanan marine ecosystem” by Dirley Cortés and Hans C. E. Larsson, 15 May 2026, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution. DOI: 10.3389/fevo.2026.1848892

Funding to DC was provided by BESS-NEO program, NSERC CREATE 46283-2015, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, and Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec (FRQNT no. 30251), and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025. Funding for HL was supported by NSERC RGPIN-2016-06725 and RGPIN-2022-04370.

#6530. Even for Desperate Restaurants, Fake Reviews Just Aren’t Worth It

A new report proves that planting fake Yelp reviews has dire long-term impacts on restaurants

When Yelp was first launched in 2004, it flopped. The company’s initial model of an email-based referral service failed to take off until its creators realized users were taking the platform into their own hands; in lieu of sending one another recommendations via email chain, they began using a “hidden” link at the bottom of the startup’s website to write unsolicited reviews of everything from doctors to restaurants. Yelp 2.0 launched in 2005, and gave those reviews a more visible place to live online — one that emboldened users to feel more authentic stewardship, by way of direct authorship, over hyping up the businesses they enjoyed (or didn’t). The startup bought a whopping 20-million-business database, and amplified a world of reviews outside of the restaurant- critic echo chamber. It was a fresh democratization of information, which was itself one of the more optimistic legacies of the Y2K internet.

It’s been over 20 years since Yelp was founded. At its best, the platform still feels like a place where the voices of hungry, curious diners can share their personal experiences and offer recommendations and tips; at its worst, it feels like a bloated repository for reviews filled with misdirected anger, unreasonable expectations, or else completely fake customer reviews. Initially, unsubstantiated and unreliable reviews were more often written by a person — either someone from the business itself, or paid by the business; now, a fake review can be penned by a paid influencer, a detailed generative AI prompt, or purchased from third-party agencies that will produce fake bot reviews in bulk.

Fake reviews were perhaps inevitable. Bot-driven comments became ubiquitous during an overripe moment in the untamed internet’s lifespan. But how does a restaurant shamed for gamifying its reviews — even if it was, presumably, out of desperation in a tough economic landscape — regain customers’ broken trust?

… The offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp.

In 2026’s AI-addled digital ecosystem, researchers are starting to understand even more about how paid-for, planted reviews impact the restaurants behind them, and whether trying to gamify platforms to achieve high ratings is worth it at all for businesses. A recently published working paper on the consequences of restaurants flagged by Yelp for fake (planted, incentivized) reviews found that since 2023, more than 4,900 businesses have been flagged with Yelp’s “Consumer Alert” banner, which exists on the penalized business’ page for a 90-day period and lets Yelp users know that the business has been caught peddling fake reviews. In 2020, the fast-casual chain Burgerim was found guilty of planting fake reviews, and received over 200 digital warning banners across its various locations’ Yelp pages.

The impacts of that digital pillory extend far beyond its 90-day duration. Yi Cao is an assistant professor of accounting at George Mason University, and the co-author of the paper; almost immediately, Cao noticed the offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp. Cao’s team cross-analyzed the business’ performance on Yelp with real-life foot traffic reports (from global location data firm SafeGraph) and credit card transaction data (courtesy of Consumer Edge), and discovered that most of the penalized restaurants struggled to recover to pre-alert traffic even after a year and a half. The stink of chicanery lingered.

While Cao says his team doesn’t know every signal that Yelp uses to identify fake reviews, they do know that it relies “substantially on reports from consumers and business owners,” and that “they also have an algorithm running in the background to screen reviews for AI-generated language — which is a sign of possible review inflation.” At this point, the cost of planting a good review is only getting steeper as the technology capable of detecting it improves. “This is a classical theory of a trade-off between the benefits of manipulating reputation and the risks of getting caught,” Cao explains, “When the risk is relatively low, the business owners decide the incremental benefits are worth the risk.”

Yelp’s real restaurant reviews don’t necessarily need to be etched in stone, but as AI-penned reviews become less detectable and more sophisticated, what diners want now, more than ever, is a human touch and a sense of authenticity.

People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming — in which the dreamer is aware that they are dreaming and can sometimes influence the dream's trajectory — is a skill that can be honed, a new study finds. And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month.

The study's results could have practical benefits, said Daniel Morris, a cognitive neuroscientist at Northwestern University who studies dreams and was not involved with the work. "Lucid dreaming can benefit people with nightmares by allowing them to transform their nightmares into positive dreams and feel greater agency in their dreams," Morris told Live Science in an email.

Before this study, published Sept. 28 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, neuroscientists tried to induce lucid dreaming with various methods. These included meditation exercises and so-called reality checks, in which participants ask themselves while awake whether unusual phenomena they encounter — such as people wearing odd Halloween costumes — are real or if they're dreaming. The idea is that they will ask themselves the same question in their sleep during bizarre dreams.

However, "for most people, our day-to-day lives may not feel 'dream-like,'" Morris said, explaining why reality checks have had mixed results and don't reliably trigger lucid dreaming.

Since dream-like scenarios are rare in waking life, the neuroscientists behind the new study used VR simulations of bizarre situations to complement reality-check exercises.

The team, based at the University of Trento in Italy, recruited university students and asked them to meditate and then perform the VR training. The meditation was intended to increase students' awareness of what they were thinking about in a given moment. Each time they encountered bizarre happenings in the VR environment, such as objects or people violating laws of physics or rapid switches from one scene to another, they performed reality checks.

After the training, participants went home and were asked to keep a dream diary that they wrote in every morning. They also filled out daily questionnaires, citing the number of dreams they recalled and how many they remembered being lucid.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The participants experienced lucid dreams four times more often than participants did in a second group that did reality checks without performing any meditation or VR training. The study also included another comparison group, in which participants carried out reality checks during realistic rather than dream-like VR simulations; these participants were over eight times less likely to report lucid dreams. This latter comparison ensured that the results were not caused solely by the use of VR, the researchers said.

When participants encountered something strange, like branches covering a door, they actively asked themselves whether it was real.

It was particularly surprising to find that such little training with the dream-like VR simulations was needed to develop lucid dreaming as a skill, said study co-author Nicola De Pisapia, a neuroscientist at the University of Trento. His team ran the experiment for only a month because any longer would have been too demanding for the participants, De Pisapia noted.

Study co-author Andrea Signorelli, a doctoral student in De Pisapia's lab, thinks the VR intervention is at the heart of why the approach worked. People often don't realize that they're dreaming because the dreams "fool" your senses and feel realistic in the moment, he explained.

"Virtual reality is the technology to fool you on stereoscopic vision and auditory information," he said. The term "stereoscopic" refers to techniques that create 3D illusions from 2D images by mimicking how human eyes see.

"It's basically the most immersive technology that we have at the moment," making it a good intervention for reality check exercises, Signorelli said.

The team also compared the number of lucid dreams participants reported against their total number of recalled dreams, which revealed an interesting pattern. On average, participants in each group recalled more dreams after starting the experiment than they did beforehand. However, the dream-simulating VR group recalled the fewest dreams overall after entering the experiment, even though they had the highest number of lucid dreams.

Signorelli speculated that perhaps it takes a lot of energy to have lucid dreams, which could divert resources away from recalling other dreams. Morris argued that, alternatively, participants in the lucid-dream VR group "may have been less motivated to report non-lucid dreams than the control groups." So there may have been some bias in the reporting.

The study had some limitations, such as its small sample size of 38 participants. Plus, neither of the two control groups were asked to meditate, so it is impossible to say whether the meditations or the dreamlike VR sessions had more influence over lucid dreaming in the test group.

The team is now doing a follow-up study in which the meditation part has been removed, Signorelli said, to reveal whether the VR dream scenarios are the critical factor, as suspected.

Signorelli said that he would like to see lucid-dream training tailored for each individual. For example, the VR simulations could be personalized to simulate a recurrent nightmare that a given person experiences, training them to recognize triggers specific to that dream, he said.

"Other future research could explore the potential therapeutic benefits of this intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety, or PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]," Morris suggested.

#6527. Food-Themed Fashion Is Starting to Feel Gluttonous

﻿The millennial avocado obsession walked so the Loewe tomato clutch could run

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

There was a time, not too long ago, when a purse shaped like a baguette felt like a thrilling — even subversive — novelty. Now, we hardly bat an eye when we see that Moschino has made a trompe l’oeil celery purse, or that Big Bud Press is making a hot-dog-and-pretzel-print jumpsuit in collaboration with a Los Angeles bar. How did we get here? And has it all become a little too much?

Fashion has long found inspiration from the culinary world, but the influx of food-fueled prints, graphics, and trompe l’oeil accessories that picked up steam during the pandemic have now reached a cultural tipping point.

The then-emerging brand made food a central theme of its vision: Its cake-topped aviator caps, Ferrero Rocher heels, and beeswax-sculpted cheese hats — hyperrealistic, absurdist food designs capable of achieving instant social media virality. Prior to working in fashion, Puppets designer Carly Mark was working as an artist whose pieces revolved around candies and snacks. As she told Business of Fashion in 2023, the Puppets universe felt like the ideal pairing given what she considers food and fashion’s motivators: pleasure and money.

During the pandemic, the much-duped “strawberry dress” took over TikTok, and Tombolo Company found a hit on its hands with its vongole shirt, which debuted in 2019, but found peak popularity in 2021. The shirt appeared in Vogue in 2020, and InsideHook called it an “obvious bedfellow to day-drinks, rooftops and weekenders” — in other words, a status symbol. Katie Kimmel’s T-shirts made chicken-parm enthusiasm akin to being a devout sports fan, and in 2022, this very publication called “seafood kitsch” the look of the summer, as items like Rachel Antonoff’s super-popular seafood-tower dress flew off the digital shelves.

Why was food so primed to become a motif in clothing at this point in culture? One could make the argument that it has roots in the millennial optimism years: Earlier in the 2000s and 2010s, the concept of “foodies” was new. Brands printed tongue-in-cheek food- and coffee-related motifs and slogans (a fervent love of avocados comes to mind) on hipster apparel, as the idea that “you are what you eat” developed growing fervor. That period was a key stepping stone in the evolution toward the far more elaborate and pervasive marketability of food-as-identity we see today. Content creator Cole Poska, who is a partner and creative director at Beyond Studios, tells Eater that “food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.” Poska’s own Instagram often reimagines restaurant merch just for fun; his designs for Cheesecake Factory apparel went viral, such as a hat that resembles the iconic brown bread. He points out that people will defend their favorite fast-food order like it’s a family member, and with the kind of loyalty that’s hard to manufacture. The same could be said about their martini order, or favorite taco spot; it’s all a way of telling others who we are through what we like.

But the fatigue is undoubtedly here. In 2024, Bon Appétit asked “Why Does Every Dress Have Pasta and Cocktail Shrimp on It?” And as the novelty factor of a shrimp-print dress has worn off, the next question might be: Will there be any true longevity for these food-as-fashion moments? Our feeds overflow with products that are hurriedly designed for flash-in-the-pan viral trends and quickly destined for a landfill; arguably more so if the object in question prioritizes shock value and gimmicks over function and brand identity.

This is undoubtedly all related to the accelerated speed of trend cycles and shortened consumer attention spans. However, as Leah Asmelash wrote last year for CNN, the rising costs of food also casts an increasingly sinister shadow over food-themed fashion. In 2026, a $425 cardigan emblazoned with oysters has waning originality compared to a few years ago; it falls into banality at best and the Hunger Games at worst; its wearer indicating that they’re financially comfortable and, more importantly, well-fed. In that light, beyond its role in identity, food has become more of a status symbol than ever. A sweater touting one’s love of caviar is shorthand for their access to and appreciation of luxury, culinary and otherwise. But sporting the mass-market Temu version? It’s more akin to wearing a faux Gucci belt.

“Food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.”

If it’s possible to escape the sense of accelerated-trend-cycle disposability, it may have to be through a more subtle approach than, say, a bag that looks like a giant stick of butter. Sam Salad is the co-founder of Meals, a Los Angeles-based, workwear-inspired apparel company that, by its own description, “bakes ‘food culture’ into apparel, blurring the lines between the clothes we eat and the food we wear.” Utility is at the forefront of Meals, which offers a classic chef pant with a slightly fuller cut, in both basic colors and subdued aesthetic homages to blue cheese and watermelon. When Meals launched in 2019, Salad was selling premium denim along Venice’s Abbot Kinney Boulevard, a hotbed of Instagrammy food culture and trendy restaurants like Gjelina that helped inspire his own brand. “Design today has to translate across languages and platforms,” Salad tells Eater.

Food is hardly a new bedfellow for fashion designers, even if today’s hyper-fast trend cycle has kicked it into overdrive. “Food is totally universal,” Salad says. “Issey Miyake once merchandised their pleats collection as little omakase sets.” He cites that collection among other fashion-meets-food moments that he considers successful, such as the iconic Salvador Dalí- and Elsa Schiaparelli-designed lobster dress. At the time of its 1937 creation, the dress was a scandal: It assumed a conformity-defying sartorial stance and was fittingly worn by Wallace Simpson. Today, its highly devolved spawn are available on Shein for $13.

As it stands, one clear way out of corny, food motif purgatory is for brands — fashion or food — to focus less on quantity and more on storytelling and quality. “We do a few things really well, and that’s enough,” Salad says, “Like In-N-Out [Burger].”

Poska’s philosophy is similar. “I’d rather make one thing people talk about for a year than 20 things people forget about tomorrow,” he says. “The first person to make a candle look like a stick of butter is a genius. The hundredth person is just making a candle.”

#6526. Trapped in Amber for 99 Million Years, a Lizard’s Tail Reveals an Ancient Survival Secret

A clean break in 99-million-year-old amber offers rare direct evidence that ancient lizards shed their tails using a defensive mechanism still common today.

A lizard can escape a predator by leaving its tail behind, sometimes with the detached piece still wriggling as the animal makes its getaway. It’s a remarkable defense, but scientists have struggled to determine how far back it goes. Ancient reptile fossils can show where a tail was capable of breaking, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean the animal could shed it to escape danger.

An unusually revealing clue has now emerged from a tiny piece of amber discovered in northern Myanmar. Measuring just 18 millimeters (about 0.7 inches) long, the amber holds a lizard’s tail that detached approximately 99 million years ago. What makes it so valuable is the remarkably preserved point where the tail separated from the body. Researchers say it provides the best-preserved direct fossil evidence of autotomy, the defensive mechanism that allows lizards to shed their tails.

For years, no one recognized what was trapped inside the amber. Dolev Fabrikant, a PhD candidate at Tel Aviv University’s New Environmental School, was examining what appeared to be a tiny twig or fragment of an insect when he noticed something unusual about its surface. “I realized that what seemed to be a twig was covered in tiny scales,” he recalls. “It was a lizard’s tail.”

Fabrikant shared his discovery with his supervisor, Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology and Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, whose reaction was immediate.

“I nearly jumped out of my chair,” says Dr. Davranoglou. “I instantly realized that this tiny fossil could open an extraordinary window into the past, helping us understand the history of one of the most widespread survival strategies among reptiles. Until now, we could only speculate on whether ancient lizards could shed their tails. We now have direct evidence that one could.”

Getting a closer look at the fossil was another challenge. The amber was cloudy, and the structures inside were too small for an ordinary microscope to reveal the details researchers needed. Rather than cutting open the specimen, the team turned to micro-CT scanning at Israel’s Volcani Institute.

“Micro-CT takes X-ray images from many angles and combines them into a three-dimensional reconstruction. It allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open,” explains Dr. Ahmed Nasser, Head of the institute’s Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.

At the severed end of the tail, the scans revealed a distinctive ring of tissue closely resembling the structure found in tails shed by living lizards. The separation itself was relatively clean and symmetrical, without the damage patterns that would be expected if the tail had broken off in an accident.

That distinction matters because other reptile fossils have offered less conclusive evidence. Some preserve natural fracture planes in the tail vertebrae, while others contain regenerated tails, indicating that the animals had lost part of their tails previously. Although these features suggest that ancient reptiles possessed the ability to shed their tails, the presence of fracture planes alone cannot establish that they actually used this defense. In the Myanmar specimen, the preserved tissue and clean separation provide much stronger evidence that the tail was released through autotomy.

The researchers still cannot determine exactly what kind of lizard left the tail behind. Without the rest of its skeleton, including the skull, there are too few anatomical clues to identify its closest relatives.

“Although we can securely identify this specimen as a lizard, we lack the skull and other skeletal features that would allow a more secure identification. Possible affinities include the groups containing today’s wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards,” says Apostolos Christopoulos, a PhD candidate at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.

How the tail ended up in amber is another mystery. The lizard might have become stuck in sticky resin and shed its tail to free itself. It is also possible that a predator attacked the animal, prompting it to release its tail, which later landed in resin.

Reference: “Direct fossil evidence of caudal autotomy in a Cretaceous lizard” by Dolev Fabrikant, Apostolos Christopoulos, Ahmed Nasser and Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, October 2026, Palaeontologia Electronica. DOI: 10.26879/1706

#6525. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6524. The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

Our favorite folders, flippers, and automatics from Benchmade, CRKT, Case, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

This guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

The Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

When testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

The Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

The D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an issue.

Coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the company also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

The wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

The flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks new.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

The satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

Benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

To me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

The design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

At under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

In terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

Benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

The Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s new Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

Part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

The other big change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a new stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

There’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade says the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

One drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

The design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Size and weight are also big differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

Overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

The CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

Another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

With three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

Testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

While I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the big one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

We update this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing new pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any new knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

Choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:

Handle material is also an important choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

The action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

In the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

If cost is a major factor for you, it will quickly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

Knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

Choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

In the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

The American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

Possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

Most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In New York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

Outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That said, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

Knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

These sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

This is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The company raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

While I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re new to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Her background is in service journalism and earlier in her career she worked as a daily newspaper reporter and book editor. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.

#6523. Common Nutritional Supplement Shows Surprising Promise Against Psoriasis

A widely available nutritional supplement may help reduce the immune system activity responsible for psoriasis, according to new research from China. Scientists found that pantethine, a derivative of vitamin B5 commonly used to lower cholesterol, can interfere with metabolic processes that drive inflammation. The findings were supported by experiments in mice and a small clinical trial involving people with psoriasis.

In the 12-week trial, 24 patients received standard treatment with topical calcipotriene/betamethasone ointment. Half also took pantethine tablets. Participants receiving the supplement showed improvements in their symptoms, particularly those who started with elevated blood cholesterol levels. Although encouraging, the results are preliminary and do not establish pantethine as an effective standalone treatment.

The research focused on dendritic cells, immune cells that help organize the body’s defenses. These cells detect and present foreign substances to specialized T cells and release chemical signals that recruit other immune cells. When dendritic cells become excessively active, they can sustain the inflammation associated with psoriasis and other autoimmune diseases.

The scientists discovered unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from patients with psoriasis and several other autoimmune conditions. Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient involved in cellular energy production. The researchers found that increased Vanin activity depleted pantethine, promoting cholesterol production within dendritic cells and triggering excessive immune activation.

“Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression,” says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. “But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.”

To investigate this connection, the researchers reduced Vanin levels in dendritic cells. Without these enzymes, the cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. A drug that inhibited Vanins also prevented the development of psoriasis in mice.

Further experiments showed that replenishing pantethine reduced cholesterol accumulation inside dendritic cells and suppressed their activation. Pantethine treatment also alleviated psoriasis symptoms in mice, providing additional evidence that the metabolic pathway contributes to inflammatory disease.

“We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins,” Zhang says.

Pantethine has long been available as a nutritional supplement because it can inhibit cholesterol synthesis. The new findings suggest that its effects on cholesterol metabolism may also influence immune responses. However, the small human trial cannot establish whether the improvements resulted from the same cellular mechanism demonstrated in laboratory experiments.

“Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation,” Zhang says. “Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell–mediated autoimmune diseases.”

Reference: “Vanin-pantethine metabolic axis shapes dendritic cell function and affects inflammatory disorder progression” by Ai-Ping Cao, Jun-Cheng Li, Rui Wang, Yun-Ying Wang, Nan Wu, Yan-Hong Liu, Zhi Jin, Jia-Yu Liu, Yan-Yan Shen, Yue Guo, Qi Qi, Yao Wang, Rui-Bo Wang, Bo-Yang Xie, Chun-Yan Yan, Qiu-Ying Han, Shao-Yi Huang, Sheng-Ming Wu, Na Wang, Xin Pan, Cheng-Xin Li, Tao Zhou, Ai-Ling Li, Qing Xia and Wei-Na Zhang, 27 October 2026, Journal of Experimental Medicine. DOI: 10.1084/jem.20252558
