#6496. The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

From wood pellets to charcoal, these cookers use a little heat and a lot of time to make incredible barbecue.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a new dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

If you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

We’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, currently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

We supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

One of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.)

It has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time issue where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how quickly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

The only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

You don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

The biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

There’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All said and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

The Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review

Masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

As with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

With 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a big boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That said, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

This Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

Some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

The Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that shows whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

In many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

When we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that shows a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

We put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

When smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford

Though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for new barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Big Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the company, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Their excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by their shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

This small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

There’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

Most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

Kamado grills, like the famous Big Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for new barbecuers.

Smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

Smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s important to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That said, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

With a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

It depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

That said, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.)

Tony Carrick is a full-time freelance writer who specializes in technology, home improvement, DIY, home security, and outdoor recreation. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6495. Students Test Prototype Landing Pad to Make Lunar Operations Safe

When spacecraft perform vertical landing and takeoff maneuvers from the lunar surface, the results are very messy! Beyond the intense heat produced by the rocket engines, the force also kicks up regolith, the particulate dust that covers most of the lunar surface. With so many crewed and cargo missions planned for the coming years, space agencies are contracting with commercial partners to develop infrastructure that will keep spacecraft, astronauts, and other surface elements safe from all "moondust."

This includes landing pads that provide a stable surface and barrier for vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) vehicles. To help them realize their objectives under the Artemis Program, NASA has enlisted engineers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) to create some. Their work is part of a multi-year partnership with Linc Research Inc., a certified engineering company located in Huntsville, Alabama, and supported through NASA's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.

The student research team is led by Dr. Judy Schneider, a professor in UAH's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Their research is focused on developing a design for modular, vented landing pads that will allow for safe transits to and from the lunar surface. This summer, the team successfully conducted three rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype of their landing pad at the university's Propulsion Research Center, demonstrating its ability to capture and redirect rocket exhaust through an integrated vent system.

Rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype lunar landing pad at the UAH Propulsion Research Center. Credit: Cadis Ammons

On Earth, landing pads consist of a solid structure capable of withstanding the full force and heat of a rocket plume. This can result in significant damage to the pad itself, as demonstrated by the first launch attempt of SpaceX's Starship prototype, including cratering beneath the mounting structure and sending debris flying in all directions. In contrast, the UAH team's design uses interlocking components with channels that help reduce thermal damage and protect the structure as well as the spacecraft.

For the tests, the team created individual concrete components and arranged them into a prototype measuring 3.65 m (12 ft) in diameter. The concrete serves as an analog for building materials that could be produced from lunar regolith, either "sintered" to form 3D-printed ceramics or combined with a bonding agent to produce "lunacrete." The components also had integrated sensors to record how the rocket plume's exhaust was channeled through the vent systems during the three firings.

The modular design also makes it easier to build on the Moon, where manufacturing centers are likely to be space-constrained. Smaller, individual components also mean future landing pads will be easier to assemble, expand, maintain, and repair over time. Combined with the use of local resources for building materials - aka. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) - the team's goal could help make large-scale lunar infrastructure more feasible.

Earth's fluffy, dense atmosphere also helps prevent rocket exhaust plumes from expanding freely and kicking up dust. Because its only natural satellite is an airless body, dust clouds caused by impacts or rockets can travel all the way to the other side of the Moon. As a result, powerful blasts during takeoff and landing can propel dust at high speeds, potentially damaging nearby habitats, power elements, equipment, and other infrastructure. The dust can also be thrown into orbit, where it could interfere with orbiting satellites, space stations, and incoming spacecraft.

This marks a major step in developing landing infrastructure that will enable a lunar base and crewed operations in the near future. As Schneider said in a UHA press release:

On Earth, we use water-cooled flame buckets to redirect rocket exhaust. But we won't have those resources on the lunar surface, where water will be in limited supply. Our goal is to redirect the rocket plume so it doesn't damage the landing vehicle or any surrounding structures. The hot-fire tests demonstrated that we could redirect the rocket plume. By using an internally vented structure, we were able to prevent the heat from damaging the pad as it could in a solid structure.

With the initial tests complete, the team is now working on a 6 m-diameter (20 ft) landing pad that will be delivered to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center (also in Huntsville) for additional testing and evaluation. These tests will further assess the design, push its technological readiness, and determine if the vented, modular approach can be scaled and adapted for repeated use. These efforts will bring the technology another step towards realization and deployment on the Moon.

Further Reading: University of Alabama Huntsville

#6494. “Schrödinger’s Penguin”: Scientists Discover a Bizarre Paradox Among Endangered Penguins

Endangered erect-crested penguins are holding steady on tiny islands while declining on a breeding ground 40 times larger, challenging assumptions about where the species’ best hope for survival lies.

An endangered penguin species could receive a less severe global risk rating even as one of its only two breeding populations suffers a steep decline. A survey of erect-crested penguins in Aotearoa New Zealand shows how a single assessment of an entire species can conceal very different conservation needs.

The erect-crested penguin is among just four penguin species worldwide listed as “Endangered” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another is New Zealand’s hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin. Yet while the hoiho has attracted sustained public and conservation attention, the erect-crested penguin remains largely overlooked and is one of the country’s least-studied penguin species.

These birds breed only on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two remote island groups about 800 kilometers (500 miles) southeast of the South Island. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers used drones to photograph and count every breeding colony across both groups, the first time this had been done for the entire species.

The study, published October 21, 2026, in PLOS ONE, was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, whose researchers are based in the Departments of Zoology and Marine Science at the University of Otago (Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka). The team collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Mattern says, “Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

“The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.”

The counts also challenged the historical view of where most of the species breeds.

“The results overturn a long-standing assumption,” Mattern says.

“The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species’ stronghold.”

The researchers have dubbed the situation “Schrödinger’s Penguin” after the well-known thought experiment in which a cat sealed in a box is imagined to be simultaneously alive and dead until someone opens it and checks. For the penguins, Mattern says, the logic runs in reverse.

“With Schrödinger’s cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

“With Erect-crested penguins, it’s the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

“Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn’t one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.”

On the Antipodes Islands, a shrinking colony may become increasingly difficult for the penguins to defend. Mattern describes how that can compound the losses.

“As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.”

The islands’ eastern rockhopper penguins had already experienced a population collapse. Their numbers crashed “catastrophically” during the second half of the 20th century, leaving fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs on the Antipodes Islands. The decline mirrored trends elsewhere across the species’ Southern Ocean breeding range and was likely driven by ocean warming.

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that this loss may have changed which penguins the predators targeted.

“As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead,” Pütz says.

Increasingly severe storms, consistent with broader climate trends in the Southern Ocean, have also triggered landslides that break colonies into smaller fragments and put them at further risk. Differences in the birds’ ocean habitats and migration routes likely add to the pressures.

Outside the breeding season, Antipodes birds travel far into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone, a region of the Southern Ocean, Mattern says. Bounty Islands birds stay close to their breeding sites in more sheltered waters that may also be more productive.

The contrasting population histories complicate how the species’ extinction risk should be assessed. According to Mattern, its current Endangered ranking rests on inflated population estimates from the 1970s. Reassessing that status against the new data broadly supports the ranking for the Antipodes population, but not for the Bounty population.

“Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to “Vulnerable”, masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species’ last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.

“A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger’s box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs,” Mattern says.

Reference: “Schrödinger’s Penguin? Divergent population trajectories and the challenge of assessing the threat status of the Erect-crested penguin” by Thomas Mattern, Klemens Pütz, Hannah Mattern, Robin Long, Dave Houston, Bianca Keys, Jeff White, Richard Seed, Myrene Otis, Ursula Ellenberg, Pablo Garcia-Borboroglu and Benno Lüthi, 21 October 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359075

The study was funded by the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust, the Global Penguin Society, and conducted under permits from the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

#6492. New Research Reveals That Honey Beehives Act as a Living Immune System

Scientists have discovered that honey beehives possess a surprisingly sophisticated system for protecting colonies against disease.

A honey bee colony relies on more than its workers to fight disease. The hive itself acts as a “living immune system,” using carefully arranged natural materials to create layers of antimicrobial protection around developing bees and stored food. New research shows that these defenses are closely linked to the surrounding landscape, with local vegetation influencing how effectively a colony can resist harmful microbes.

“Hives are not only homes for bees, but also act as their workplaces, restaurants, and hospitals, and now we can add immune systems to the list,” said lead researcher Dr. Kenya Fernandes.

The strongest antimicrobial defenses were found in parts of the hive most exposed to the outside environment. Honey showed particularly powerful antimicrobial activity, while propolis, a sticky plant-derived substance bees use to seal cracks and openings, provided additional protection. Both materials contained biologically active compounds, including hydrogen peroxide in honey and plant chemicals called flavonoids in propolis.

Deeper inside the hive, where eggs and larvae develop, the defenses became more selective. Beeswax combs, stored pollen, and substances produced by the bees themselves helped suppress harmful bacteria and fungi while supporting beneficial microbial communities.

“As we travel closer to the hive center, the antimicrobial defenses became more targeted, with wax comb, stored pollen, and the bee’s own bodies helping to filter out harmful bacteria and fungi, while encouraging helpful species,” said Fernandes, a 2026 NSW Tall Young Poppy Award recipient.

“We already know honey, beeswax and propolis have antimicrobial properties independently. But what came as a surprise was how these materials were placed in the hive wasn’t random, but organized. The hive’s antimicrobial properties worked together to protect the eggs and larvae, as well as the fermented pollen the bees consume.”

For the study, published in ISME Communications, scientists examined 24 honey bee colonies across five apiaries at Tocal College in New South Wales, Australia. They analyzed the chemical composition and antimicrobial properties of honey, pollen, beeswax, and propolis. They also investigated microbes living in the bees’ digestive systems and tested the antimicrobial activity of their tissues and secretions.

The researchers found that many microorganisms in hive materials likely originated from floral nectar. Colonies located closer to native bushland also showed measurable differences in chemical defenses compared with those near agricultural land. These differences suggest that the plants available to foraging bees influence the protective properties of the materials they bring home.

“This shows healthy hives depend on and are influenced by healthy ecosystems. Land clearing and intensive farming could be quietly eroding the bees’ natural defenses. This builds a strong case for protecting diverse flowering habitats that support healthy hives,” said co-author Elizabeth Frost, Technical Specialist Bees at the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD).

The hive’s protective system was generally more effective against bacteria than fungi. Researchers suggest this imbalance may reflect the greater threat posed by certain bacterial infections. One example is American foulbrood, a highly contagious disease that kills honeybee larvae and can destroy entire colonies.

“There are direct threats to bee populations such as the varroa mite, but many don’t realize the indirect threats: the shrinking of healthy ecosystems has a domino effect. Landscapes with diverse plant species can increase the bees’ chances of being resilient to disease.”

The findings also raise questions about other colony-building insects. Although the study focused on European honey bees, Fernandes hopes to investigate whether Australian native stingless bees have comparable nest-based defenses and whether similar systems occur in other social insects.

“I’d love to see if other social insects such as native stingless bees, ants, and termites, which also build incredibly complex homes, also have the same system,” Fernandes said.

Reference: “Spatially organized chemical defences shape microbial communities in honey bee colonies” by Kenya E Fernandes, Aviva Levina, Elizabeth A Frost and Dee A Carter, 19 October 2026, ISME Communications. DOI: 10.1093/ismeco/ycag247

Funding: Australian Research Council, New South Wales Bushfire Industry Recovery Package Sector Development Grant

#6491. A Virtual Lifeless Earth Will Help Scientists Find Life on Exoplanets

In the search for life elsewhere in the galaxy, astronomers sift through exoplanet discoveries looking for ones that could be habitable. That means rocky planets with atmospheres in habitable zones. But one thing stymies these efforts. Can we examine atmospheres and differentiate between an exoplanet that's habitable and one that's actually inhabited?

That's difficult, partly because exoplanets are so far away, and also because we only have Earth to guide us. It's the only habitable and inhabited world we know of. But new research shows how we can work with those facts to try to detect inhabited worlds.

The work is "A Whole-planet Model of the Earth without Life for Terrestrial Exoplanet Studies," and it's published in The Planetary Science Journal. The lead author is Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who was a postdoctoral astronomy student at the University of Washington when conducting this work.

"As the only known habitable (and inhabited) planet in the Universe, Earth informs our search for life elsewhere," the authors write. "Future telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will soon look for life on rocky worlds around Sun-like stars, so it is critical that we understand how to distinguish habitable planets from inhabited planets."

Observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will inject new energy into the search for life. They will shift exoplanet science from identifying worlds that could be habitable, to identifying worlds with atmospheres showing signs of life. But as the researchers point out, we still don't know how to tell inhabited worlds, if there are any, from those that are merely habitable.

"Earth is currently the only known inhabited planet in the Universe, and geological evidence suggests that it was habitable with liquid-water oceans for most of its 4.54 Gyr history," the authors write. "Owing to its long-term habitability, Earth serves as the template that guides our search for biospheres elsewhere."

The researchers tackled this issue by building a sort of virtual Earth, but one without life.

"As a first step toward answering these questions, we present a coupled interior-atmosphere evolution model of the Earth without life from 50 Myr to 5 Gyr that reproduces 19 key observations of the preindustrial Earth after 4.5 Gyr within estimated measurement uncertainties," the researchers explain. Those 19 observations included atmospheric CO2 and H2O, surface temperature and albedo, ocean mass, and even factors like upper-mantle temperature and upper-mantle heat flow. These non-biological factors all shape a planet's atmosphere and have to be accounted for.

"Though exoplanet interiors themselves will likely never be directly observable, the effects of interior evolution are apparent in the composition of the atmosphere and the albedo of the surface environment, both of which HWO will observe on Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars via reflected-light spectroscopy," the authors explain.

This schematic shows some of the key processes included in the abiotic Earth model. Remotely observable quantities (surface temperature, albedo, and atmospheric H2O and CO2) are in bold. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

The researchers also produced reflected light spectra of the model Earth that covers the likely wavelength range of the HWO. They used a code to compute a "synthetic HWO reflected-light spectra (0.2â2.0 Î¼m) for the true Earth and the abiotic Earthâs atmospheric state after 4.5 Gyr," the authors write. These included line absorptions for CO2, H2O, O2, O3, and CH4.

This virtual Earth without life can serve as a benchmark to compare with detailed atmosphere observations of habitable worlds.

âThis model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,â lead author Gilbert-Janizek said. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanetâs atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.â

This schematic shows the atmospheric sources and sinks that define the new volatile cycling processes in the model. Fluxes related to CO2 are color-coded magenta, and fluxes related to H2O are color-coded teal. The schematic doesn't include ocean chemistry. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

Gilbert-Janizek didn't start from scratch. Senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy, had already built a model that included the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation. This work added the surface and the atmosphere to build a more comprehensive model.

The authors hope that this model can serve as a kind of plug-and-play model that can be adjusted to fit with any particular exoplanet being studied. They can input factors like albedo and atmospheric CO2 and test what happens. If the model then recreates the observations of the planet, it suggests that the exoplanet in question is uninhabited.

Naturally, an undertaking of this size and complexity requires some assumptions. The model initializes after Earth's magma ocean solidified, and that dictated the atmosphere's initial composition. The authors say they chose an initial set of conditions "that apply after the bulk of the mantle has solidified."

They also assumed that plate tectonics were active during all of Earth's history beginning in the middle Hadean, which is widely believed to be true and in line with evidence. There are alternative hypotheses saying that this wasn't the case. One says that plate tectonics only began when it shifted from a stagnant-lid to modern plate tectonics during the Archaean, but the researchers avoided that.

Other assumptions were made regarding atmospheric pressure, the strength of Earth's geodynamo, and even atmospheric escape of hydrogen. But these types of assumptions are a normal part of science and are explained up front.

But the virtual Earth model successfully reproduces the properties of the Pre-Industrial Earth, and that's the most important thing. It also predicts that a planet can maintain habitable conditions for a long time without requiring the presence of life. This is relevant because false positives are one of the HWO's challenges.

These are three Engineering Architecture Concepts (EACs) for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Each one features a different mirror design. EAC-1 is a 6m, segmented, off-axis telescope. EAC-2 is the same but uses a round keystone mirror and surrounding segments. EAC-3 is an 8m on-axis telescope with round segments. Not shown is the extendable, protective barrel that each design has, which will protect the mirror from micrometeorites. Image Credit: NASA Goddard/Conceptual Image Labs

âDr. Gilbert-Janizekâs work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,â Barnes said. âAfter more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earthâs core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate.â

The question "Are we alone in the Universe" can be asked in one breath but not answered in one. It has to be broken down to much smaller questions asked and answered across many generations. Even "Are we alone in the Milky Way" is far too large and encompassing a question. "Are we alone" has to be asked exoplanet by exoplanet, and that requires tools of the sort developed by Dr. Gilbert-Janizek and her colleagues.

Our first 6,000 exoplanet discoveries were bulk discoveries. But the search is becoming more targeted toward Earth-like planets, meaning tools like this one are becoming more and more necessary. The upcoming HWO, if it gets built, places this point in even finer focus.

âRealizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists,â Gilbert-Janizek said. âIâm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe.â

#6490. The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That said, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

In comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

Beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

The Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

The Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

While the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

The Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review

The next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

The multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

The classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

Though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

As a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

The side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

Rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

These include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

Perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

The multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

The Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

With its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

One of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

It’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

We recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

One of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too big. That said, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

Can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

We designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

We cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

During these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was said and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

For testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. #6489. Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The speed and angle of impact would have destroyed most organic compounds from comets

Comet McNaught shines over Australia a safe distance from Earth in this photo taken in 2007. Most comets that collided with the early Earth would have been moving too fast and at too steep an angle for prebiotic molecules to survive the collision and kick off chemical processes that gave rise to life, a new study suggests.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.

Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.

But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.

In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.

The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.

“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” says Anslow, who performed the research while at Cambridge University. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”

Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.

A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.

While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

This story was updated on November 5, 2026 to add Richard Anslow's prior affiliation. Anslow is now at the Met Office, but did this research while at Cambridge University.

#6488. Giant Impacts Help Rocky Planets Retain Their Atmospheres

Earth's formation was a messy process. It all happened about 4.5 billion years ago, in our young chaotic Solar System. Rocky planetesimals were whizzing around in the Solar System back then, and Earth formed as more of these objects collided and merged with it.

Some of these collisions were giant impacts that generated immense heat. These were common in the later stages of Earth's formation, after the protoplanetary disk had largely dissipated and atmospheric accretion was complete. Planetary scientists have wondered how young planets like Earth could've held onto their atmospheres near the end of their accretion period. The massive heat from giant impacts should've driven primordial He/H atmospheres away. But new research suggests that simple picture doesn't capture some important details, and that giant impacts could've actually helped young rocky planets retain their atmospheres.

The work is titled "Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The authors are Darius Modirrousta-Galian and Jun Korenaga. Modirrousta-Galian is a former Yale postdoc who is now at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Korenaga is a professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

This research focuses on what happens near the end of a rocky planet's accretion process, after the protoplanetary disk has largely dissipated. This is when other planetesimals had also grown large through their own accretion processes, and when they collided with a planet like Earth, they released an enormous amount of energy.

âGiant impacts are a key part of how rocky planets grow,â said co-author Korenaga. âPlanets the size of Earth or larger are expected to form through collisions between smaller planetary bodies. These collisions add mass and release enormous amounts of heat, which can drive atmospheric escape. Their effect on a planetâs atmosphere depends on how those two changes work together.â

Modirrousta-Galian and Korenaga have been working on how planetary interiors and atmospheres evolve together and have published several papers on the topic. Their previous research laid the foundation for this work.

Their work shows that increased heat near a planet's surface isn't the only result of impacts. Some of that heat is driven deep into the planet. The impact can also "increase atmospheric gravitational binding," according to the researchers.

There are two components of a giant impact: heat and mass.

This illustration shows planetesimals in a disk around a young star. Rocky planets grow by accretion of planetesimals, and as time goes on, the planetesimals become more massive. When these massive planetesimals impact young planets, they not only generate heat, they add mass. Image Credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech.

When a planetesimal smashes into a rocky planet, the heat can be divided into two separate components. Some of it is driven more deeply into the planet where it won't drive away the atmosphere. Some of it will be mantle heat that does contribute to driving the primordial atmosphere away. But the mass gained by the accretion of the planetesimal isn't divided. All of that mass gives the planet more power to hold onto its atmosphere.

"Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature," the authors explain. "Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactorâs metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth."

"Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention," the researchers explain.

This understanding can help explain the exoplanet population.

Astronomers used to think that our Solar System was an archetype of how other solar systems would look. There would be rocky planets in the inner Solar System, gas giants further out, and ice giants beyond them. But exoplanet discoveries have cast doubt on that. The most common types of detected exoplanets aren't even represented in our Solar System: super-Earths and sub-Neptunes.

Astronomers think that super-Earths and sub-Neptunes could represent two types of planets that started out as rocky cores but ended up with much different atmospheres. Super-Earths have lost their atmospheres, while sub-Neptunes have retained more of their primordial atmospheres. A sub-Neptune only needs to retain a few percent of its H/He atmosphere to have an extended puffy atmosphere that can increase its radius by a large amount.

These are artist's impressions of the super-Earth Kepler-452b (right) and the sub-Neptune Kepler-22b (left). They're very different from each other, and both types of exoplanet are abundant in exoplanet discoveries. Giant impacts could explain their abundance. Image Credit: NASA.

âWhy nature produces both types in such abundance is a fundamental puzzle in exoplanetary science,â said Modirrousta-Galian. âWe set out to find an explanation.â

This research shows that sub-Neptunes could have grown larger through more massive impacts, and those impacts not only added mass but allowed them to retain larger atmospheres. Super-Earth's weren't subjected to those same massive impacts, and so did not gain enough mass to retain their atmospheres the same way that sub-Neptunes did. They lost theirs due to stellar radiation.

This schematic shows different outcomes for rocky planets. In one scenario, massive impacts onto a rocky create a more massive planet that can retain more of its primordial atmosphere: a sub-Neptune. In the other scenario, there are no massive impacts, no increase in rocky mass, and the planet retains less of its atmosphere. Image Credit: Darius Modirrousta-Galian

"Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth," the researchers explain. "By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths."

These results appear to overturn the long-held idea that giant impacts spelled doom for planetary atmospheres, and in turn, for the prospects of habitability. Primordial H/He atmospheres themselves didnt create habitability. But some research shows that they're essential for the development of a world that is eventually habitable, through interactions with a young rocky planet's magma ocean. These interactions may have been a significant source of Earth's water and could be on other rocky worlds, too.

âThis overturns the decades-old canonical view that giant impacts almost always lead to complete atmospheric loss, demonstrating instead that these collisions can play a crucial role in the formation of sub-Neptunes,â Korenaga said.

#6487. Scientists Sound the Alarm As Colorectal Cancer Reverses a 20-Year Decline

Colorectal cancer rates in the United States are rising across a much wider range of ages than previously recognized, reversing a long period of declining diagnoses. A new study published in NEJM Evidence found that the increase is no longer concentrated among adults younger than 50, with rates now climbing in people approaching their 70s.

Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths overall in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. As more generations reach ages when the disease becomes increasingly common, researchers warn that growing numbers of diagnoses could place additional demands on cancer treatment and long-term survivorship care.

Researchers led by Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, analyzed National Cancer Institute data to track changes in colorectal cancer incidence over more than two decades. The age-adjusted rate dropped from 55.2 cases per 100,000 people in 2000 to 36.7 in 2022, before increasing to 38.3 in 2023.

“This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years,” Murphy said. The study also found rising incidence across age groups through 65 to 69 years, indicating that the trend extends well beyond the younger populations that have received much of the attention.

The increase among older adults is particularly concerning because colorectal cancer screening has historically produced substantial benefits in these age groups. Rates are now rising among people ages 65 to 69 and have stopped declining among those ages 70 to 74, despite approximately 80% of people in these groups being up to date with screening. Researchers suspect that unidentified risk factors may be counteracting some of the progress achieved through earlier detection and prevention.

Murphy believes the expanding age range reflects a phenomenon known as the “birth cohort effect,” in which people born during particular periods experience different disease risks as they grow older. In this case, evidence suggests that individuals born in the 1960s and afterward may face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer that persists as they advance into middle and older adulthood.

“I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time,” Murphy explained. “As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we’re going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.”

The pattern could help connect the growing incidence among younger adults with the increases now appearing in older populations. American Cancer Society statistics show that colorectal cancer incidence among people ages 20 to 49 rose approximately 3% annually from 2013 to 2022.

“There are many unique challenges when you’re diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it’s important that we shine a spotlight on that problem,” Murphy said. “But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.”

The steepest increase occurred among adults ages 45 to 49, whose colorectal cancer incidence rose by 12.76% annually between 2019 and 2023. Researchers believe this unusually rapid increase largely reflects expanded screening following a change in national guidelines that lowered the recommended starting age from 50 to 45.

Screening can temporarily raise reported incidence by detecting cancers that were already present but had not yet been diagnosed. “That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do — it’s catching cancer earlier,” Murphy said.

However, increased screening cannot fully account for the broader rise across age groups, especially among older adults who already have high screening participation. The researchers also examined whether disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the trend. The increase persisted even when data from 2020 and 2021 were excluded, and screening activity had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels by January 2021. These findings suggest that pandemic-related delays are unlikely to explain the overall increase observed in 2023.

The underlying causes of the rising incidence remain uncertain. Researchers are now examining whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could contribute to colorectal cancer risk, although no specific exposure has been established as responsible for the observed trends.

“These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced,” said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Murphy is collaborating with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to investigate thousands of environmental chemical exposures using small blood samples. This approach will help identify substances that may warrant closer examination.

The researchers then plan to work with Kupfer to study selected chemicals using colon organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce some features of human colon tissue. These models will allow scientists to investigate how particular exposures affect colon cells and potentially identify biological processes involved in cancer development.

Until the causes become clearer, colorectal cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify the disease early and prevent deaths. Current national guidelines recommend routine screening for adults at average risk beginning at age 45 and continuing through age 75. Screening decisions outside that range should be individualized based on factors such as family history, symptoms, and other medical conditions.

Colonoscopy remains the gold standard because it can both detect cancer and remove precancerous polyps. Other screening methods include home-based stool tests and newer blood-based tests, although their capabilities and recommended testing intervals differ.

“There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated,” Kupfer added.

For adults younger than 45 who do not qualify for routine screening, recognizing possible warning signs is particularly important. Blood in the stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, and unexplained weight loss should prompt medical evaluation, even in people without a known family history or genetic risk.

The research team also recommends continued monitoring of national cancer registry data as new figures become available. If the upward trend persists as large generations of Americans grow older, healthcare systems may face increasing demand for cancer treatment, follow-up care, and long-term support for survivors.

Reference: “Colorectal Cancer among U.S. Adults, 2000–2023” by Caitlin C. Murphy, Folasade P. May, Sonia S. Kupfer, Xin Hu and Samir Gupta, 27 October 2026, NEJM Evidence. DOI: 10.1056/EVIDpha2600217

The study was supported by funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.
