#6382. Scientists Found the One Thing Stress Is Actually Good For

It sounds counterintuitive, but cortisol produced by stressful situations can strengthen memory.

Stress is so unavoidable that we often have no choice but to laugh as it slowly and inevitably consumes us. Despite how often it might make us want to force a smile as we scream into the abyss, stress has some positive side effects, including how it releases the often-demonized hormone known as cortisol. Late-night infomercials blasting the newest pill or concoction to reduce cortisol production are missing something: the hormone they’re so eager to suppress has a hidden upside. It turns out that cortisol helps us hold on to memories.

Not all stress is bad. When the brain detects a stressor, it triggers a short-term biological response known as fight-or-flight. The body can handle these episodes as long as they’re balanced by downtime, like a good night’s sleep. Chronic stress, which can drag on for months or years, is often damaging. But short bursts of stress can actually enhance memory, thanks to the cortisol they release. Scientists already knew cortisol was linked to memory, but now a team of Yale University researchers has dug deeper to learn why some memories fade while others live rent-free in our heads indefinitely.

“Stress powerfully influences what we learn and remember, prioritizing encoding of emotionally arousing and stress-relevant memoranda at the expense of neutral content,” the researchers said in a study recently published in Science Advances. “These benefits are related to increased levels of stress-related hormones.”

Emotional memories form in two steps. First the brain flags an event as emotionally arousing, then it encodes that event for long-term storage so it can be recalled later. Cortisol influences both steps. When something emotionally arousing happens under stress, the brain redirects resources toward processing it, which changes activity across its entire network of neurons. Previous studies have shown that cortisol can strengthen the effects of arousal-related neurons. Oddly, high arousal on its own can impair memory, but the same arousal paired with stress can enhance it. The brain also uses different networks for emotional memories than for neutral ones, and cortisol may change how the networks tied to memory and arousal interact.

The Yale team set out to pin down exactly how cortisol affects the strength and staying power of memories. Participants took either a hydrocortisone pill (a pharmaceutical form of cortisol) or a placebo. They then viewed a series of potentially emotional images while a functional MRI (fMRI) scanner recorded their brain activity, and they rated how each image made them feel. Because fMRI tracks blood flow and oxygen levels to show which brain regions are most active and how that activity shifts over time, the researchers could see which images most strongly activated the regions involved in emotional reactions. The next day, participants were tested on how well they remembered each image. Then they repeated the entire experiment.

To see how cortisol shapes memory, the researchers searched the scans for brain networks whose activity predicted either how emotionally aroused participants felt or which images they would later remember. Some networks predicted both. Cortisol had a consistent effect on both kinds of networks, but it affected each kind differently. While memories were being encoded, cortisol made the arousal-predicting networks stronger and more stable. The most stable were the frontoparietal network, which helps coordinate behavior, and the visual network. Cortisol also strengthened the connections between networks and enlarged the networks that predicted emotional arousal.

Cortisol changed the brain’s memory networks, too. Under cortisol, both the networks that predicted memory and the networks that process emotion looked different than they did under placebo. Cortisol also increased the overlap between the networks that predicted memory and those that predicted arousal. In participants who took cortisol, the networks that forecast which images would be remembered also gave priority to storing emotionally arousing information. This hints at one way the brain adapts to stress.

“Cortisol alters memory-predictive circuits, tuning them to prioritize encoding of emotionally arousing stimuli and bringing them closer to arousal-predictive circuits,” said the researchers. “Although further studies are needed to test this framework, these results provide key insights into the internetwork dynamics by which cortisol tunes successful emotional memory formation.”

#6381. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 5: Smoke out the Southern Cigar

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tonight’s target is a bit of a test: How far south can you see? At a latitude of 40° north, NGC 55 in Sculptor — also called the Southern Cigar Galaxy or the String of Pearls Galaxy — only rises about 10° above the southern horizon at its highest, which occurs around 9 P.M. local time. Observers farther south will see it higher in the sky, while those farther north will see it closer to the horizon or be unable to make it out at all.

For those observers who can catch it, NGC 55 is a bright, 8th-magnitude edge-on barred spiral located just under 4° northwest of magnitude 2.4 Alpha (α) Phoenicis in Phoenix, which sits below the galaxy as you look south around this time of night. This galaxy is not only bright, it’s quite large, stretching roughly the width of the Full Moon (½°) at its longest. It is quite thin, however, only some 6’ wide along the other dimension. You’ll immediately see that its nucleus is not in the center, but offset to the west. Several other bright knots of star formation may also be visible within the galaxy’s plane — particularly if you drop in a nebula filter.

#6380. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6379. Where does consciousness begin? A new theory points deep inside the brain

A brainstem theory of consciousness puts the raw feeling of being 'you' in the brain's ancient stalk, and its evidence starts with pain.

Consciousness is often linked to the cortex, the brain’s wrinkled outer layer, which helps us understand language, recognize faces, and make plans.

Yet a surgeon who stimulates that layer in an awake patient can reliably produce flashes of light, sounds and tingling, and almost never pain.

Two neuroscientists now propose that the raw feeling of being conscious, the “me inside,” is computed somewhere else.

Their candidate is the brainstem, the ancient stalk at the base of the brain. The case rests on pain, and it is a hypothesis built from existing evidence, not a new experiment.

The cortex, they propose, works out what you are seeing and hearing. A small region of the brainstem, they suggest, determines what you consciously feel.

Marshall Devor of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem laid out the argument with Mark Baron, a neurologist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.

Close your eyes and cover your ears, they wrote, and “you” are still there, 100 percent.

Electrical stimulation of the visual cortex during brain surgery makes patients see light. Stimulating the hearing and touch areas produces sounds and tingling.

The neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield wrote in the 1950s that only very rarely did a patient use the word pain to describe the result of cortical stimulation. His observation still holds, Devor and Baron wrote.

One exception is a buried cortical region called the insula.

In one study the authors cite, stimulating it evoked pain at only 8 of 313 sites tested. Painful auras are rare in epilepsy too, and pain rarely appears in dreams.

Damage points the same way. Lesions in the visual cortex cause blindness, but no cortical removal anywhere prevents pain from being felt, Penfield wrote.

If anything, the authors wrote, cortical strokes can add chronic pain rather than remove it. Yet those patients remain conscious.

Small strokes in specific parts of the brainstem can cause coma, the authors note.

Devor and Baron also point to adults with hydrocephalus who remained fully articulate despite extreme thinning of the cortex.

The authors’ own rat work narrows the spot. The team microinjected a a general anesthetic into rat brains 828 times, in 182 animals.

The drug knocked the rats out only when it landed in one small region of the brainstem, the mesopontine tegmentum.

Doses of 10 billionths of a liter or less worked within seconds, and injections slightly off target didn’t.

Destroying that small area alone did not cause coma, so the authors wrote that it isn’t the whole story.

Somewhat larger lesions centered on it did, in a region about an eighth of an inch (3 millimeters) by a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters). That region, they wrote, matches where strokes cause coma in people.

In the authors’ model, the cortex does the heavy processing: telling a rhinoceros from a cloud, or a snake in the grass from rustling leaves.

It also works out whether what it sees is good or bad for survival, and it sends that verdict down to the brainstem.

The brainstem circuit then determines which information enters awareness.

If the new input matters more than whatever “you” are attending to now, it marks that stream of cortical processing as conscious.

The rest keeps running unattended, like a self-driving car.

“We humans are sentient robots,” the authors wrote. Pain skips the round trip, because signals from nerve fibers that detect potentially harmful stimuli already flag a threat.

Devor and Baron also offer an evolutionary reason.

The mammalian neocortex had not yet evolved when fish and reptiles emerged, and the ability to feel pain, they propose, arose early as an add-on to escape reflexes.

In their account, the later evolution of the mammalian neocortex built on the brainstem’s existing machinery for conscious experience.

The brainstem theory of consciousness is a framework, not a mechanism.

Hundreds of theories of consciousness exist, the authors wrote, and none of them, their own included, explain how neurons produce subjective experience.

Devor and Baron claim only that the mechanism is biological and that it has one location.

Could a fish, a reptile, or even an invertebrate feel pain without a cortex? The authors suspect so but wrote that there is no sure way to know.

Researchers cannot directly confirm subjective experiences in people or animals unable to describe them. In the rats, the team measured anesthesia and sleep, not feeling.

Devor and Baron propose studying the mesopontine tegmentum and its connections directly.

The lab’s earlier work mapped which of that region’s neurons send axons up toward the cortex and down the spinal cord.

Whether any of those cells carry the signal that turns processing into experience is the question the theory leaves open.

The hypothesis was presented in the journal The Neuroscientist.

A Roman-era belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest hints at the ancient conflict between the Romans and the Dacians.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

From Augustus to Nero, see how much you know about ancient Rome's famous leaders with our Roman emperor quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6377. Researchers discover the clever tactics octopuses use to fit through holes much smaller than their bodies

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through a gap far narrower than its body. It often does that in the wild to escape predators and…

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through a gap far narrower than its body. It often does that in the wild to escape predators and to catch prey.

In a recent study, scientists have deciphered the exact, step-by-step method that common octopuses squeeze through tiny holes.

One arm goes through first. Several more follow, and then the arms that are already through push against the wall around the hole and pull the rest of the animal after them.

When the hole was narrower than the distance between an octopus’s eyes, the animals added a step: every arm went through before the head and body did.

Wenci Xin, a mechanical engineering researcher at the National University of Singapore, and colleagues filmed three common octopuses at a public aquarium in Vienna.

Then the team tracked every arm, frame by frame. The whole-body squeeze had never been broken into steps before, the team wrote.

The three were young animals, caught by fishermen at La Ciotat in France and kept at the Haus des Meeres, the Vienna aquarium. A clear acrylic wall with one adjustable hole split their tank.

An octopus has a capsule of cartilage around its brain, and the distance between its eyes is a good guide to how big that capsule is. So the team used that distance as each animal’s size.

The smallest octopus, with eyes 0.6 to 0.8 inches (15 to 20 mm) apart, got a hole about as wide as a penny, 0.8 inches (20 mm) across.

The two bigger ones, with eyes 1.2 to 1.4 inches (30 to 35 mm) apart, got a hole 1.2 inches (30 mm) across. That’s about the width of a soda bottle cap, and narrower than the distance between their eyes.

Each animal made three to five attempts a day on three separate days. If an octopus seemed unwilling to go on, or jetted water, a stress response, the team stopped and waited at least three days.

Cameras recorded 33 attempts. Three failed when the octopus damaged the apparatus trying to get out another way, which left 30.

Every squeeze started the same way. The octopus pushed one arm through the hole, bending it into a U at the opening. Then the arm stretched out on the far side.

Michael Kuba of the University of Naples Federico II, who helped run the new work, had seen that reaching move before. In a 2015 study, Kuba and colleagues filmed octopuses reaching one arm through a hole.

Next, more arms followed the first, with shorter reaches, until they filled the hole almost completely. The team calls that shifting. Three to five arms went through at this stage, and four was the most common number.

The last step was the squeeze itself. Two of the arms on the far side twisted around and attached their suckers to the wall. By stiffening and pushing against the wall, they pulled the remaining arms, the head, and the body through in one motion.

At the wider hole, that was the whole routine, and the smallest octopus used it in all 14 of its attempts.

The two bigger octopuses, with a hole narrower than the distance between their eyes, did something different at the last step.

First the octopus rotated its body upward, which forced the bases of the arms already in the hole deeper in and opened up a little more room.

The remaining arms then twisted and stretched through, with the arms on the far side pulling, until all eight arms were through.

Once the arms were across, the octopus turned back to its normal position, with only the head and body left on the starting side.

The second pull worked like the first one: two arms attached to the wall pushed against it, and this time only the head and body came through.

From the side, the cameras caught the body narrowing before it went through. The hole pressed the body narrower, and the octopus narrowed it further on its own, the team wrote.

Those two octopuses used this four-step version in 15 of their 16 attempts.

In an interview with Earth.com, Xin said the team had expected the same strategy at both hole sizes, with the arms pushing against the wall to pull the animal through.

“We were surprised when we found that the strategy changed,” Xin said. “However, after thinking about it carefully, we felt that it was understandable, as the animals were still following the same general pattern, while the new strategy simply divided the sequence in which the body was pulled through into separate stages.”

The octopuses favored their four front arms, and the two on the left most of all. Counting from the front, the second left arm went first in 47% of the 30 attempts, and the first left arm in another 28%.

The arms that followed were usually the ones next to the probing arm. At the wider hole, the two arms at the ends of that group consistently did the pulling.

At the narrower hole, when the second left arm had probed, the first right arm and the fourth left arm nearly always pushed the body through.

The team also tested four-month-old juveniles of a second species, the Mexican four-eyed octopus. Offered a hole 0.4 inches (10 mm) wide, no wider than the distance between their eyes, the young octopuses did not try it. Two Mexican four-eyed octopuses given a penny-wide hole used the three-step routine every time.

Offered a 0.6-inch (15 mm) hole beside two 0.4-inch ones, one animal tried a narrow hole first. It got one arm through, then two more, and could not get any more through. After several failed tries it moved to the wider hole and went through in three steps.

Robots built to search collapsed buildings have to fit through gaps in the rubble, so they’re built narrow, and a narrow body leaves little room for equipment, Xin said. Engineers make the robot longer instead, which is why so many rescue robots look like snakes.

“If we could develop a squeezable, octopus-inspired robot, such a design could accommodate a larger range of functional components while retaining access to confined spaces,” Xin told Earth.com.

Each of its eight arms could do the job of one slender rescue robot, carrying sensors, tools, or communication devices.

Cecilia Laschi of the National University of Singapore supervised the work. Laschi and Kuba co-wrote a 2015 paper on a soft eight-arm robot that moves and grasps underwater like an octopus. The hard part of a soft robot like that is control.

An octopus arm can bend anywhere along its length, so there’s almost no limit to the ways it can move. That makes it hard to control. So is a robot arm built the same way.

The authors suggest the octopus keeps control simple by reusing a few standard arm moves and organizing them into one motion.

The moves are a bend, a stretch, a twist, and a stiffening. The footage can’t prove it, they wrote, because the moves varied from one attempt to the next.

Each of the three octopuses was tested at only one hole size. So the authors can’t say whether the extra step came from the hole size or from the individual animal’s own preferences.

The octopuses’ preference for their left arms may come from the tank itself, the team wrote: one side of it gave the animals a clearer view out.

And the cameras were aimed at the arms and the head, not the body, so how much the body narrows to fit has not been measured.

The usual assumption has been that the beak sets the limit on how small a hole an octopus can get through.

The failed attempts suggest the limit may also depend on how thick all eight arms are together where they join the body. An octopus may not be able to tell whether it will fit before it tries.

Xin called the work an initial study with many open questions. “For example, can this behavior harm the animal, and what determines the smallest opening an octopus can squeeze through?” Xin explained.

The next step the authors propose is a larger group of octopuses, with each one tried at more than one hole size.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

#6375. Study of nearly 200,000 adults shows that eating snacks after dinner greatly increases the risk of liver disease

A study of nearly 200,000 adults links late-night eating to a much higher rate of liver disease, though direct causation remains unproven.

People who snacked after dinner or after going to bed had a 20 to 30 percent higher rate of liver disease than those who did not, according to researchers at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). The finding comes from nearly 200,000 U.S. adults followed in three long-running health studies.

The conditions included fatty liver disease and cirrhosis, a serious form of liver scarring.

The research is observational and relied on habits that participants reported themselves. A follow-up study at the same university will now test whether eating earlier helps.

Earlier research had already tied late-night snacking to heart disease and obesity, the OHSU team noted. The researchers set out to see whether the same habit was also tied to liver problems.

Robert Wilechansky, M.D., a hepatologist at OHSU who specializes in liver transplantation, is the study’s lead author.

Night shift workers, whose day-night cycle is out of step, have higher rates of both conditions. That pattern led Wilechansky to wonder whether small changes in meal timing could make a difference.

“A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease,” Wilechansky said.

His co-authors include Kevin Casey, Andrew Chan and Tracey Simon of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. OHSU announced the results on October 9, 2026.

The team analyzed three large, preexisting nationwide datasets. Two came from the Nurses’ Health Study, established in 1976, and the Nurses’ Health Study II.

Across three generations, the nurses’ studies count more than 280,000 participants.

The third source was the Health Professionals Follow-up Study. Launched in 1986, it enrolled 51,529 men working as dentists, pharmacists, optometrists, veterinarians and in other health professions.

Those men answer health questionnaires every two years and detailed diet questionnaires every four years.

Participants self-reported their diet and lifestyle habits, including whether they ate late. The team defined late-night eating as eating after dinner or after bedtime.

People were grouped by eating behavior. The researchers then looked for correlations with reported cases of MASLD or cirrhosis.

The first condition was metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD.

In MASLD, excess fat builds up in the liver for reasons other than heavy drinking, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).

The institute estimates that about 24 percent of U.S. adults have MASLD. OHSU puts the share of Americans affected at as much as 30 percent.

Overweight or obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and abnormal blood fats all raise the risk, the NIDDK lists.

In a more severe form, fat comes with inflammation and damage. That form may lead to cirrhosis, the second condition examined, in which the liver is scarred and permanently damaged.

Cirrhosis can in turn lead to liver cancer. Yet MASLD is usually silent, and even cirrhosis can develop with no symptoms.

“We know the liver is very much in tune with the body’s circadian rhythms,” Wilechansky explained. “So we’re interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health, without changing the composition of what people eat.”

Andrew McHill, Ph.D., an associate professor and sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU, is a co-author.

“We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it’s sleep, eating or exercise, really matters,” McHill said.

“For example, we have shown that eating during the night, when the internal biological clock is promoting sleep, reduces the ability of your body to metabolize foods as efficiently and can eventually lead to obesity, diabetes and now poor liver health,” he continued.

The analysis does not prove that late eating damages the liver. It shows an association between eating times and later diagnoses.

Wilechansky cautions that the findings come from observational, broadly defined, self-reported data.

The authors place their results within wider research on late eating and metabolic health.

Wilechansky is part of an OHSU team now recruiting for a new study. It will monitor eating behaviors directly and test whether eating earlier improves clinical measures of underlying MASLD.

“It’s important to remember, of the people who developed fatty liver disease, only a small fraction develop serious forms of the condition like liver cirrhosis,” Wilechansky noted.

“Even so, the big take-away here is that confining your calorie intake to several hours before bedtime might be beneficial,” he added.

The study was published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

#6374. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

EST. You can spot the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up. Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6373. A 4,000-year-old wall was found hiding underneath a Moroccan ridge that a French archaeologist sketched in the 1930s

Charcoal beneath a wall Armand Ruhlmann recorded in 1936 at Oued Beht, Morocco, dates its first phase to as early as 2010 BC.

In 1936, the French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann published photographs and a sketch of the walls on a ridge at Oued Beht, in Morocco’s Khémisset Province. He took them for a prehistoric enclosure. Under the stones he described, a wall dated about 4,000 years old remained buried.

It turned up in a trench dug by hand across the largest wall during the 2023 field season, which ran from October 30 to November 17. Charcoal from its cobble foundation gave a radiocarbon range of 2010 to 1747 BC.

The trench belongs to the Oued Beht Archaeological Project, with partners in Rabat, Rome and Cambridge. Its results are now out in Libyan Studies.

The paper reports a ditch, an earth bank and a wall from the early to mid-second millennium BC, and it leaves their purpose open.

Four stone alignments run east to west over the southern end of the ridge, above a river that flows all year. The village of Aït Siberne shows to the east in drone photographs taken by Toby Wilkinson of Cambridge.

Ruhlmann tied the biggest alignment, now labeled Wall B1, to a slighter wall on the western scarp and to Wall C further south. He read them as an éperon barré, or barred spur. That is a headland closed off on its open side by a rampart.

Giulio Lucarini of Italy’s National Research Council and Cyprian Broodbank of Cambridge are the corresponding authors of the new paper. They and 19 co-authors call Ruhlmann’s plan a “neat but unproven reconstruction.”

A French and Moroccan project dug into Wall B1 and Wall C between 2013 and 2015. That work is unpublished, and the remnants of its trenches were still open in 2022 and 2023.

Local residents told the team that the upper stonework had been bigger within living memory. The wall had also been turned into a stable for animals.

Trench 3 was laid out as a long slit across Wall B1. Its northern extension, Trench 3.1, was offset to keep clear of an olive tree. Work there stopped at about 4 feet (1.2 meters) for safety.

The visible wall, numbered F.300.2, is about 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) wide at ground level and 4.4 feet (1.35 meters) high. It is built of limestone blocks and cobbles in compacted earth.

Under it lay F.300.1, an older structure of burnt and unburnt daub, a building mud, with ashy lenses full of charcoal. It sat on rounded river or beach cobbles less than 4 inches (10 centimeters) across. All 17 sherds from it were prehistoric.

A second charcoal date, from the burnt material, gave 1896 to 1623 BC. The authors link that layer to the destruction of the first wall.

The team had expected Wall B1 to widen the site’s time range. “This expectation was spectacularly fulfilled,” the authors wrote.

North of the wall, Trench 3.1 ran into a ditch parallel to it. It was about 6 feet (1.84 meters) wide and at least 2 feet (65 centimeters) deep, and its base may not have been reached. One of its fills held a polished stone axe, and all 18 sherds from the ditch were prehistoric.

Bulk soil samples of 10 to 20 liters (about 3 to 5 gallons) went through flotation, which lifts seeds and charcoal off in water. Three charred seeds of domesticated crops from the ditch came back at about 1500 to 1300 BC.

The lowest phase of the earth bank gave 1532 to 1424 BC and 1497 to 1300 BC. A slanted posthole north of the wall, probably for a timber prop, held a legume seed dated to 1502 to 1324 BC.

Altogether the two trenches produced 17 dates, eight on seeds and nine on charcoal. Two charcoal samples with modern results were treated as intrusive and set aside.

The wall line follows the contact between Jurassic dolostone on the south and the Blue Marl Formation on the north. In their conclusions, the authors call the Wall B1 sequence “the earliest such constructions confirmed in the region.” Defense is one reading, but other motives for enclosure “cannot be excluded at this stage,” they wrote.

An earlier paper in Antiquity dated a farming community on the northern ridge to about 3400 to 2900 BC. Its authors called it currently the earliest and largest agricultural complex in Africa beyond the Nile corridor.

After the 2023 survey, that settlement is put at 10 to 11 hectares (25 to 27 acres). It has yielded bell-shaped storage pits, painted pottery and polished stone axes. Plant remains include barley, durum wheat, pea and wild olive.

In the second millennium BC, the activity moved south to the narrow tip. Morocco is better known for far older material, such as shell beads 142,000 to 150,000 years old and hominin jawbones from Casablanca.

The paper sets Oued Beht next to Kach Kouch, a site near the Mediterranean coast. People lived there late in the second millennium BC.

The authors suggest the two may mark a Bronze Age in northwestern Morocco, in step with the Argaric culture, a Bronze Age society in southern Spain. In those centuries, a fire at Cabezo Redondo in Spain preserved a wooden loom.

Medieval builders went back to the same line. Charcoal from the middle phase of the bank gave two dates in the 11th to 12th centuries AD. A stone wall just north of Wall B1 gave the 11th to 13th.

The standing stone wall belongs to that later phase, according to the paper, because the upper layers of the bank probably went up at about the same time. A seed from the fill inside the wall gave 1729 to 1516 BC, which the authors put down to older soil reused as fill.

At the northern edge of the site, local people had reported human remains in 2022, during house building. The team dug three test trenches there. Trench 7 exposed a burial with its skull to the west, and a molar dated it to the 13th century AD.

Across a shallow valley, about 1,640 feet (500 meters) away, survey walkers found a dense spread of 11th to 13th century pottery on a hilltop. One sherd, painted cobalt blue, was likely made in Fez.

Wall C, the southern piece of Ruhlmann’s plan, has no dates. Whether the three walls ever formed one enclosure is still unknown.

A copper-based rod 2.2 inches (5.5 centimeters) long came from the bank south of Wall B1. Its layer has no radiocarbon date, and no Bronze Age metal has been confirmed at Oued Beht so far.

Each radiocarbon date gives the earliest possible age of its layer. Charcoal and seeds can predate the soil that buried them.

Ruhlmann’s 1936 sketch showed Wall B1 as a rampart of unknown age. Its first phase now has two charcoal dates, and the authors have proposed limited work on Wall C.

The project runs under a memorandum of understanding between Morocco’s National Institute of Archaeological Sciences and Heritage, the National Research Council of Italy, ISMEO (the International Association for Mediterranean and Oriental Studies) and Cambridge’s McDonald Institute. The paper thanks the Oukhayi family for letting the team dig on their property.

The full study was published in the journal Libyan Studies.

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. #6371. Researchers hung baited cameras off a boat and identified 50 different oceanic whitetip sharks using only their fins

Baited cameras off Cat Island, The Bahamas, filmed 50 oceanic whitetip sharks that researchers told apart by dorsal fin markings over two seasons.

In late April 2023, a Florida International University (FIU) crew off Cat Island in The Bahamas started dropping baited GoPro cameras over the side. The goal was to film oceanic whitetip sharks about 43 feet (13 meters) down, with 2 pounds (1 kilogram) of bonito as bait.

They came back in 2024 and did it again. By then the video showed 50 separate whitetips. Each one was picked out by the notches, shape and pigmentation pattern of its first dorsal fin, the tall fin on the back.

Candace Fields, who is Bahamian and got her PhD in marine biology at FIU in 2025, ran the survey. Counting fins sometimes put up to three times as many sharks at a camera as the usual tally. All of it, though, comes from one island and two springs of fieldwork.

According to NOAA Fisheries, oceanic whitetips can reach 11 feet (3.4 meters). They spend most of their time in the top 656 feet (200 meters) of the open ocean.

NOAA puts the drop across the Pacific at about 80 to 95 percent since the mid-1990s. It names bycatch in commercial fisheries and demand for the fins as the main threat, and says some recent recovery is possible in the Pacific.

A Mote Marine Laboratory report found that most species in the shark fin trade are threatened with extinction. The IUCN lists the oceanic whitetip as Critically Endangered, and the U.S. Endangered Species Act lists it as threatened.

Yannis Papastamatiou is an FIU marine biologist at the university’s Institute of Environment and one of Fields’ advisers. “When you’re talking about marine predators in the ocean, that’s very difficult to answer, much harder than with terrestrial predators,” he told FIU News.

“If you want an idea of the abundance of lions, you can do airplane surveys and count them. But in the marine environment, you can’t see things, so that’s very difficult to do.”

FIU researchers had already surveyed another shark species for 10 years at an atoll with baited cameras, FIU News reported. Off Cat Island the water was too deep to anchor cameras to the bottom.

Fields tried two kinds of rig in late April and early May of 2023 and 2024. One was a frame of 3/4-inch galvanized steel pipe holding at least two GoPro Hero9 Black cameras. It drifted on a rope under a float and a flagged marker buoy, with a dive weight underneath.

The other was a wire bait cage with a camera. It hung about 49 feet (15 meters) from a 79-foot (24-meter) Viking sportfishing yacht. In the acknowledgments, the authors thank Captain Scott Genereux for running the Lady G.

The crew put out 99 sets between Columbus Point and Tartar Bank, a shallow seamount west of the island. Of those, 76 hung from the boat and 23 drifted, each at least half a mile (800 meters) from the last. Whitetips came to 51 of them.

Some earlier accounts said whitetips home in on boat engines. In this survey the tethered cage drew no more sharks than the drifting rig. Whether the engine was on or off did not matter either.

More sharks turned up at Columbus Point, a shelf edge where tuna, wahoo and billfish feed in winter and spring. Windy days brought more of them too. The authors think the rigs drifted farther and the scent of bonito spread wider.

Fields told FIU News that reading whitetip fins is similar to reading the spots on a whale shark. In the Western Indian Ocean, photos of those spots helped track individual whale sharks over ten years.

Until now, whitetip photo ID came from divers, who could swim into position for a clean shot. “In a video survey, obviously, you have no means to control how the shark approaches the camera. So, one big question was: is this even viable?” Fields said.

Each time a whitetip came into view, an annotator saved a still of its first dorsal fin. A shark got its own code, such as OWT1, only once both sides of the fin were on camera.

Some sharks circled the rig again and again. Others swam in at angles that hid the markings, and glare and murky water hid more. Still, the team picked out at least one shark by its fin on 41 of the 51 sets with whitetips.

Twenty-five of the 50 sharks got full codes. The other 25 were told apart from the right side of the fin alone.

Twelve sharks were filmed on two or more sets in the same season. Two of them, OWT8 and OWT15, were first filmed in 2023 and came back to the cameras in 2024.

Most camera studies report MaxN, the largest number of one species seen in a single frame. The fin count and MaxN agreed on about 87 percent of sets. Most of those had no whitetip or just one.

With two whitetips on screen at once, the counts matched only 31 percent of the time. With three, it was 28 percent. Papastamatiou said fin IDs let a researcher review the footage and say “actually, that was three different sharks.”

Fields now works at the Cape Eleuthera Institute in Rock Sound, Eleuthera. “I think what FIU did for me was solidify the importance of coming back home to work. The Bahamas is a big hub for shark research, and there are little to no Bahamians involved in that work,” she told FIU News.

Her other adviser, Demian Chapman, now works at Mote Marine Laboratory in Sarasota, Florida. Fields said both men pushed her to stick with it and become a Bahamian shark expert.

The 99 sets are a first count for whitetips in The Bahamas. They say nothing yet about whether the population is rising or falling.

On some sets no fin could be read. In those cases the team used MaxN. On three sets it told sharks apart by sex, a tag or fishing gear hanging from the body. The data are not in a public archive, and the paper says Fields will share them on reasonable request.

The authors also note that The Bahamas is a shark sanctuary but whitetips swim out of it into fished waters. In the Marshall Islands, scientists found that a shark sanctuary offered little protection from illegal fishing.

Next, the team wants cameras at more points along the archipelago, to see whether the sharks stay put or travel between islands. Fields also hopes to add photos from citizen scientists to the fin catalog.

OWT8 and OWT15 first swam up to the bonito off Cat Island in the spring of 2023. A year later both were back.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Biology.

#6370. The Secret to Your Quarterback’s Arm Isn’t Just Luck or Athleticism. It’s Physics, Expert Explains.

A physicist breaks down the mechanisms of a perfect pass. You’ll never watch a game the same way.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

It’s Sunday afternoon on September 27. The play clock is winding down. San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy takes the snap and looks downfield. Receiver Mike Evans breaks toward the end zone, but the Cardinals’ defenders are closing in. Purdy releases the ball. It arcs above the turf, drops into the receiver’s hands, and the crowd roars. How did this seemingly perfect pass come together? Along with skill and strength, some fascinating science was at work.

Crucially, the quarterback needs to identify his intended receiver and get the football to the right location at exactly the right time. This split-second decision requires an implicit understanding of several important principles of physics, including projectile motion, speed, launch angle, angular momentum, and air resistance. Put this all together, and you might just clinch a seamless play.

As a physics lecturer at Clemson University in South Carolina, I spend my days analyzing the science that makes your favorite sports possible. For instance, in my Physics of Sports course, we seek to break down anything from ski jumping to boxing to pole vaulting, and this analysis is a sample of what that process might look like. Understanding these nuances completely reshapes how students watch games—and perhaps it will do the same for you.

Let’s start with some assumptions so we can cover the basics without additional variables: We will ignore air resistance for now and assume the quarterback and receiver will contact the ball at the same height. Once the football leaves the quarterback’s hand, it continues moving in the same direction because of its inertia, or the tendency of a moving object to stay in motion until a force changes its motion. Without gravity, the ball would continue moving in that upward direction forever. However, gravity pulls the ball downward as it flies, causing it to gradually slow on its upward trajectory. Eventually the ball reaches its highest point, the upward motion momentarily stops, and the ball accelerates as it falls back toward Earth.

The ball’s horizontal motion is very different because it maintains the same speed as it travels parallel to the field. Together, these vertical and horizontal motions create the ball’s familiar curved path, a parabolic trajectory. The shape of the trajectory depends on the speed and angle with which the quarterback throws the ball.

You might think that, to have the ball travel farther downfield, a player must throw it faster. However, it’s the trajectory that is key.

A low-angle throw (around 15 to 20 degrees) follows a relatively flat trajectory and therefore reaches the receiver quickly, though this enables defenders to intercept, because the ball travels close to the field. Alternatively, the quarterback can release the football at a higher angle (such as a throw at 50 degrees), producing a more pronounced arc. A greater launch angle allows the ball to travel above the reach of opposing defenders for much of its flight; however, it may not make the ball travel any farther downfield because more of its initial speed is directed upward and less is directed forward.

The trade-off in launch angle choice is that with greater throwing angles, more of the ball’s initial speed is directed upward rather than horizontally, increasing the time the ball spends in the air. While this can help the quarterback throw over defenders, it also gives both teams more time to react.

An interesting quirk of projectile motion is that complementary launch angles—two angles that add up to 90 degrees—produce the same horizontal range, provided the initial speeds are identical. For example, a football thrown at 30 degrees and one thrown at 60 degrees will travel the same distance downfield. However, the 60-degree throw will rise higher and remain in the air considerably longer. If the quarterback wants to maximize the distance of a throw, pitching the ball at a 45-degree angle produces the greatest horizontal range, because it balances the ball’s forward and upward motion to maximize its time in the air and its downfield travel.

Quarterbacks practice throwing balls with speed, which they can couple with a low launch angle to create a bullet pass. This type of pass travels low to the ground and the reception is completed very quickly, with the advantage that the opposition has very little time to reach the ball. To throw a ball as far as possible, the quarterback would choose to throw the ball as fast as possible at that aforementioned 45-degree angle.

So far, we know the quarterback can control the speed and angle of the pass—but that precision is all for naught if the ball isn’t heading toward someone who can catch it. In other words, the quarterback must be able to adjust these variables to make sure the football arrives in the right place at the right time.

Let’s imagine a receiver running a route that requires him to sprint downfield, change direction, and then break toward the sideline. The quarterback must anticipate how long it will take the receiver to reach the intended catching location. This depends on several factors, including the receiver’s running speed, route length, and any defensive traffic that might slow him down.

Knowing approximately how many seconds it will take the receiver to reach the anticipated location, the quarterback selects a throwing speed and an angle that delivers the football at that same moment. The quarterback is solving a timing problem: The motion of the football and the motion of the receiver must intersect at the same location at the same time. Spacecraft mission planners solve a similar issue when they chart where the moon will be when a spacecraft arrives, ensuring the two reach the same place simultaneously.

Experienced quarterbacks often throw before the receiver reaches the intended spot. After years of practice, they’re able to anticipate where the receiver will be when the ball arrives, rather than aiming at the receiver’s current position. If the timing is off, fans often gripe: “He just threw it away!”

As if controlling the speed, angle, and timing of a pass weren’t challenging enough, the quarterback also controls how the football rotates during flight. When a quarterback throws the ball well, it spins around its long axis, from point to point, stabilizing the football as it flies.

The physics principle behind this stability is conservation of angular momentum. A spinning football tends to resist changes to the orientation of its axis of rotation, which helps to prevent excessive wobbling during flight. This is the same basic principle that causes a spinning top to remain upright. When the top is spinning rapidly, it resists tipping over. However, as it slows down, the top becomes less stable and eventually begins to wobble and fall.

A football behaves similarly. Its spin helps maintain a stable orientation, allowing it to move through the air more efficiently. Although up to this point we have disregarded air resistance, aerodynamic forces do influence the ball’s orientation. Without sufficient spin, the football may tumble or wobble, increasing aerodynamic drag and making its flight less predictable.

Games don’t happen in a vacuum. Everything we’ve discussed thus far becomes even more complicated when we account for real-world conditions. On an actual football field, wind and air resistance—or drag—can significantly influence the ball’s motion.

If the quarterback is throwing into a headwind, the football experiences air resistance, which slows its forward motion because the oncoming air exerts a drag force opposite the ball’s motion through the air. To compensate, the quarterback may need to increase the throwing speed or adjust the launch angle to ensure that the ball reaches the intended receiver. On the flip side, if the wind is blowing in the same direction as the pass, it may help the football travel farther, requiring the quarterback to use slightly less throwing speed.

A crosswind creates another challenge. Wind blowing from the side can push the football away from its intended path. The quarterback may need to aim slightly upwind so that the football drifts toward the desired catching location.

Sudden gusts of wind are particularly difficult because they can change the football’s trajectory after it has already left the quarterback’s hand. He can no longer make corrections, and the ball may end up off course.

A quarterback’s throw depends on more than arm strength. The quarterback must judge the ball’s speed and direction, choose a launch angle, and account for the receiver’s movement and the ball’s spin, all while adjusting for environmental conditions. Then the quarterback must bring those decisions together in a controlled throw. Although quarterbacks don’t consciously solve projectile motion equations during a game, years of practice allow them to develop an intuitive understanding of these relationships.

In terms of a game, this might look like the following: Brock Purdy throws a beautiful spiral downfield, Mike Evans races toward the predetermined spot, and the quarterback’s prediction becomes a catch! The result may look effortless, but physics is at work from release to reception—and now you’ll never watch a game the same way again.

#6369. Nov. 5, 2006: Mars Global Surveyor goes quiet

Designed to study Mars in a comprehensive way, examining its atmosphere, its interior, and its surface, the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) launched Nov. 7, 1996. By Sept. 12, 1997, it would reach Mars and slip into orbit around the Red Planet. Over the next nine years, it revealed an evolving world of ongoing geological dynamism, analyzed the history of water on Mars, tracked the movements of ice at its poles, and analyzed its topography and weather. With nearly 200,000 photos captured, MGS supplied more images of Mars than all the missions before it – combined. It also helped NASA plan for future rover missions to the Red Planet.

MGS substantially exceeded its two-year mission, but on Nov. 2, 2006, the orbiter signaled to NASA that it was experiencing difficulties with its solar panels. Two days without communication followed. On Nov. 5, more signals were sent, and then MGS went silent. The mission officially ended on Nov. 14, with NASA concluding a battery failure had caused a computer error that closed out MGS’s tour.

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6367. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6365. Curiosity captures a martian dawn

The morning Sun casts a hazy glow over Mars’ Mount Sharp, lighting up distant wind-carved rock formations known as yardangs. This scene is cropped from a six-image panorama captured by the Mastcam on NASA’s Curiosity rover at 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 11, 2026, the mission’s 4,982nd sol (martian day). Mount Sharp, formally Aeolis Mons, stands 3.4 miles (5.5 km) tall at the center of Mars’ 96-mile-wide (154 km) Gale Crater. Since 2014, Curiosity has climbed roughly 0.6 mile (1 km) up its stratified slopes, reading each new layer like a chapter of martian geology.

The mountain’s lowest, oldest layers likely formed from sediment deposited by lakes and streams that have long since vanished. This photo is the most detailed view to date of the much younger yardang layer. Of particular interest is the fact that the color and orientation of the yardangs don’t match the surrounding material. Scientists think these features could have been built up from volcanic ash that settled after a nearby eruption, and was then carved away by the wind. Curiosity should reach the yardangs’ base in 2027, where its instruments will help uncover how the layer formed.

A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

Adriani et al. (2026). Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NET/ORCA. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. https://doi.org/10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012
