#6363. Weather Guard’s Pack Rat Turned My Nephew's Pickup Into a Rolling Workshop

Instead of digging through tool bags and loose hardware at every stop, the Pack Rat Drawer Unit kept everything organized, secure, and within easy reach—making every job site a little more efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Let’s start with a bit of transparency here: When Weather Guard sent me its Pack Rat truck toolbox, I thought it was destined for my new Honda Ridgeline. Then reality set in. While the Ridgeline is a fantastic daily driver and weekend project truck, its composite bed and in-bed trunk make it a poor match for a permanently mounted contractor toolbox. That trunk alone is a vehicle highlight, so burying it beneath a steel monolith seemed almost criminal. So instead of writing a review based on specs alone, I handed the Pack Rat over to someone who actually needed it—my nephew, a newly minted electrician who spends his days hauling electrical tools, fittings, wire, and hardware from one job site to the next.

A few hours after we installed it into his pickup and began organizing his gear, it became obvious this wasn’t just another truck accessory. It fundamentally changed how he uses his truck.

Picture a broad, low steel box bolted to the pickup bed’s floor, with a single wide drawer that pulls out over the lowered tailgate. The model we tested measures 60 inches long by 49½ inches wide, and stands 9½ inches tall. At that expanse, the top of the box system essentially becomes the new carry bed of the truck, sitting just about level with the wheel wells.

That measurement is something to be mindful of if you carry a lot of taller cargo. Trucks vary in cargo bed depth, so you’ll have to subtract 9½ inches from the overall depth of your bed to know the remaining height to the top of your bed rails. The top of the bed rails on my nephew’s Chevy Silverado 1500 sits at around 21 inches, so he still has a substantial 11½ inches to carry cargo.

To that end, for the model we tested—the 369-3-04—Weather Guard rates the top for up to 2,000 pounds evenly distributed. The drawer itself has a separate 425-pound capacity. That’s a lot of weight. It should be noted that your truck’s payload limit still applies to the combined weight of the box—about 300 pounds—its contents, and any cargo on top.

The Pack Rat is less a toolbox and more like a mobile organization system. Beneath the steel top, a massive full-width drawer rides on a set of internal rollers that allow it to glide smoothly in spite of the load within. Fully loaded with cordless tools and hardware, the drawer never sagged or bounced once. To that end, we thought pushing it shut would be a chore, but the drawer rolled back in with little effort, closing with an authoritative thunk that spoke to the solid overall build quality. It’s the kind of rolling momentum that reminds you to keep your fingers clear–not because it’s flawed in any way, but because it’s built with serious heft.

Organization is where the Pack Rat really makes its mark. Four walls fixed across the drawer space are separated by 24 adjustable divider panels. This allows you to tailor the drawer layout to fit your needs instead of forcing your tools into compartments of predetermined size. My nephew dedicated one side almost entirely to his Milwaukee cordless tool collection–drills, impact drivers, oscillating tool, batteries, and chargers–while configuring the remaining space to hold electrical supplies that change from job to job. Connectors, wire nuts, fittings, fasteners, electrical tape, and specialty tools all have designated homes, making it immediately obvious when he is in low supply on any item.

Weather Guard also paid attention to the details outside the drawer. The top surface is lined with aggressive grip tape, providing secure footing when climbing into the truck bed on damp mornings or during inclement weather. It seems like a small touch until you realize you’ll be stepping on this box as a platform throughout the day.

Before installing the Pack Rat, my nephew would often toss fittings, connectors, and hand tools into half a dozen different bags and bins. Now everything lives in one place, where it stays dry as a bone. He spends less time digging through piles of tools, knows exactly where everything belongs, and can get back to work faster. For professionals whose trucks serve as rolling workshops, those small gains in efficiency translate into real money saved over the course of months and years.

The Pack Rat is unapologetically designed for tradespeople–or at least serious enthusiasts whose vehicles are dedicated to their everyday work life. It’s a substantial piece of equipment, and that comes with trade-offs. The heavy-gauge steel construction adds noticeable weight to your vehicle, which will inevitably have some impact on your vehicle’s fuel economy. Installation is more involved than dropping, say, a Tmat organizing system or cross-over box into the bed since it’s meant to stay put. Furthermore, once installed the box consumes roughly 7 to 8 inches of vertical bed space. The tradeoff, of course, is that you retain the entire footprint of the bed above it. But if you frequently haul taller gear or equipment, that’s something to consider.

For the right buyer, though, those compromises will likely fade into the background. For years, my own truck was my office, my warehouse, my livelihood—even my diner most days. So it would have been a joy—and a value add—to have the Pack Rat at that stage of my work life. At the end of the day, having every tool, fastener, and accessory protected, organized, and within arm’s reach isn’t just convenient—it’s a real productivity upgrade.

#6361. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

New findings suggest that "food challenges" can help prevent children from being saddled with unnecessary allergy diagnoses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A peanut allergy diagnosis in infancy can mean years of avoiding the food or undergoing treatments to build tolerance. But a recent study suggests that more than one-third of babies thought to have the allergy may stop reacting badly to peanuts within months of that diagnosis.

In an analysis published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice, researchers conducted supervised "food challenges" with infants diagnosed with a peanut allergy. These challenges involved giving the babies increasing amounts of peanut protein, with the intention of confirming whether they indeed had an allergy.

The team found that more than 1 in 3 infants who underwent the food challenge tolerated the peanut protein, meaning they didn't experience symptoms of an allergic reaction.

"This rate is much higher than we thought," study co-author Dr. Timothy Brettig, a pediatric allergist at the National Allergy Centre of Excellence in Australia, told Live Science.

Between April 2024 and October 2025, Brettig and colleagues retroactively reviewed the medical records of 1,275 infants who had been referred to Australian public hospitals after having a reaction to peanuts before their first birthday. These babies had first been assessed by allergy specialists at a median of 10 months of age.

For their initial diagnosis, the babies had to have a history of an allergic reaction to peanuts and show evidence of peanut sensitization on an allergy test. These tests included a skin-prick test, in which peanut extract is placed on the skin before it's lightly pricked, to check for a local reaction; and blood tests that detect antibodies against peanut proteins.

"Children under 1 year of age are an interesting group, as their immune system is still in rapid development and existing allergy tests may not reflect their allergic status well," said Dr. Alexandra Santos, a professor of pediatric allergy at King's College London who was not involved in the study. While these tests can hint that a child is sensitized to certain foods, they don't necessarily confirm that a baby will have an allergic reaction upon eating said food; the tests can also give false positives.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Of the 1,275 infants, 778 later underwent a food challenge roughly six months after their first recorded allergic reaction; at that point, their median age was 13 months old. They were given up to seven gradually increasing doses of peanut protein, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams. These doses were given at 15-minute intervals while medical staff monitored the children for signs of an allergic reaction.

Nearly 35% of the participants — 271 kids — completed the challenge without reacting.

"This is an excellent article," said Dr. Drew Bird, a pediatric allergist at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center who was not involved in the study. "The take-home message is to strongly consider a supervised oral food challenge when an infant's peanut allergy diagnosis is uncertain."

Bird emphasized that these challenges should ideally be done before a child starts oral immunotherapy, a treatment in which patients regularly consume carefully measured amounts of the food they are allergic to. The dose is gradually increased under medical supervision, with the goal of helping the patient tolerate greater amounts of the allergen and reducing the risk of reactions from accidental exposure.

An incorrect diagnosis can prompt families to unnecessarily avoid exposing their children to peanuts.

The starting dose is often determined through a similar oral food challenge to the one used in this study, though. So in theory, that challenge would help reveal whether the child needs treatment in the first place.

Bird cautioned that food challenges should be performed by a board-certified allergist-immunologist and an experienced allergy team in a setting equipped to treat anaphylaxis — a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.

In this study, 507 infants reacted during the food challenge, and of those, 61 developed anaphylaxis and were treated with epinephrine (the hormone in EpiPens).

"In an ideal world, with infinite resources," Santos said, "all patients except for those with a history of severe reactions would have a food challenge for diagnosis."

Because that is not the case, the families of infants whose allergy diagnosis is uncertain may be advised to avoid peanut products while they await a formal food challenge, she noted. But in the interim, they may miss an opportunity to help the child develop tolerance and, in turn, increase the risk that their allergy will persist.

Food challenges should be prioritized for infants whose allergy diagnoses are uncertain, she said. This would include babies who have low levels of peanut-specific antibodies in their blood or who show only small welts on skin-prick tests.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Brettig, T. W., McDonald, E., West, D., et al. (2026). An oral food challenge is required for accurate diagnosis of peanut allergy in infants prior to oral immunotherapy: Evaluation of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Pathway to Tolerance Peanut Oral Immunotherapy Program. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaip.2026.08.044

#6358. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6357. This Snapmaker 3D Printer Makes Multicolor Prints Faster—and Wastes Less Filament

Affordable, efficient multi-toolhead printing brings your prints to life.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The Snapmaker U1 revolutionized multi-material 3D printing when it launched in late 2025, introducing a clever toolhead swapping system that speeds up the process of switching between colors or materials, while minimizing the waste it normally generates.

Most 3D printers use a single nozzle to lay down layers of plastic, but the U1 features a set of four nozzles, each of which pulls from its own filament feed. When it’s time to change color or material, the printer swaps the entire toolhead automatically, which takes about five seconds—up to four times faster than most single-head printers can change colors. The mere concept garnered record-setting support in the U1’s pre-release Kickstarter campaign. It helped that, at $750, it was far more affordable than any other multihead printer.

And, upon testing, it turns out that the printer is everything Snapmaker’s supporters hoped it would be. I added the U1 to our guide to 3D printers earlier this year based on some initial testing, but have now had it in my lab for about a year.

The multihead system is indeed faster and more efficient, and U1’s user interface makes it a genuine pleasure to use. Since my initial testing, a new technology called “full spectrum printing” has come out that greatly expands the options for multicolor printing, especially for multi-toolhead printers like the U1.

All of that only reaffirms the U1’s place among my favorite printers right now: It’s an easy recommendation for anyone looking to upgrade or even get their start with 3D printing, especially if you plan on making multicolor or mixed-media prints.

The Snapmaker U1 is a CoreXY printer, which means that the print heads move left and right and forward and back, while the bed moves up and down. (As opposed to a “bed-slinger” that moves the print bed forward and back, while the print head moves up and down.) The toolheads are held on a rack at the back of the print chamber, and all four sides have windows, which makes it easy to visually monitor your prints.

It produces crisp, detailed prints with minimal fuss. Between my initial testing and recent revisit, I logged over 165 hours of print time, creating models of all shapes and sizes, from small, intricately detailed miniatures to large vases and accessories for my table saw and shop vacuum.

Snapmaker provides a free, reskinned version of Orca—a popular “slicer” program that breaks down 3D models into layer-based blueprints for printing. It’s also compatible with any slicer software you prefer. I had issues with the speed of Snapmaker’s slicer when I first tested the U1 last year, but I’m happy to report that the latest versions of the software run more smoothly.

The model I tested did not have a top lid. This is fine for filaments with lower print temperatures, such as PLA (polylactide), but can be an issue if you want the more durable prints that require higher temperature or foul-smelling filaments. Snapmaker currently offers an add-on lid and HEPA/activated carbon air filter for $150, allowing you to have more control over the internal temperature of the chamber, and to control fumes from printing. But even with the lid, the Snapmaker U1 has no active chamber heater—it relies on the heat from the nozzle and bed to maintain the chamber temperature. This means printing high-temperature filaments like ASA (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate) or ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) can be difficult. (If this is an issue for you, consider our Best for Durable Prints pick, the Bambu X2D.)

The defining characteristic of the U1 is its four separate toolheads, and its efficiency during multicolor or multimaterial prints. A 3D printer with a single toolhead can create multicolor prints, but it’s a laborious process. To switch colors, the printer needs to clip the current filament, purge any excess material from the nozzle, then feed in the next filament. And it will go through that full process on every single color switch. A complex print may have several hundred filament changes, which will add long stretches of inactivity, as well as mounds and mounds of waste. That’s why it pays to spring for a multi-toolhead printer. They can swap among a limited number of colors without changing filaments, minimizing time and material losses.

To demonstrate the difference, I printed the left and right cheeks of a mask on the Snapmaker U1 and the Bambu P2S, our current Best Overall printer. (The models were identical, only mirrored to more easily tell one from the other.) While the P2S excels at standalone printing, the difference in print material and time is staggering.

Even in a small, hand-sized print, it makes a huge difference. On a larger or more complex job, you could save a meaningful amount of money (by keeping your filament on the spool).

That efficiency when swapping colors makes the Snapmaker U1 particularly well-suited for one of the newest developments in multicolor printing: Full spectrum printing, which allows the printer to blend filament colors by laying down thin, semi-translucent layers of filament on top of each other to create a wider array of colors, much like an ink-jet printer.

Traditionally, 3D printers cannot create or control color: The color (or colors) of your materials are your only options, and you need to have spools of filament for every color you want to use. Even with four printer heads, that can be fairly limiting. After years of using 3D printers and dealing with all the labor and waste around switching colors, the ability to blend colors feels shocking in the best way possible. It’s absolutely liberating.

Since full spectrum printing was developed as an open-source technique, it isn’t exclusive to the U1; but it was developed with this printer in mind. And the full spectrum technique of applying many thin layers of filament means that it’s ideal for use with a multi-toolhead printer like the U1. Snapmaker’s slicer fully integrates full spectrum printing, meaning that you can begin using it at no cost.

It’s worth noting, though, that other manufacturers are hot on Snapmaker’s tail, releasing their own tool-changing printers and embracing full spectrum technology. But, for now at least, full spectrum printing makes the U1 a wonderfully distinctive choice, capable of doing a lot of things that most other 3D printers can’t. (At least not without wasting a metric ton of filament).

Of course, all the technical bells and whistles don’t mean a thing if the printer itself is so difficult to use that it sits idle. Luckily, the U1 has a user-friendly design that frees you up to focus on making things, rather than endlessly tweaking poorly labeled settings, or scouring the internet for solutions to what should be a simple issue.

The U1 is more intuitive than most printers, and that’s clear right from the moment you unpack the machine. The U1 comes with an extensive, step-by-step assembly document, with full-color images of each step and a QR code that links to a video walkthrough. I loved that it shipped with extra parts, so a broken part doesn’t bring you to a complete standstill until you order a replacement. And the U1 comes with a generous amount of starter filament, with 500 grams of four colors, compared to most printers that ship with only a few grams, enough for no more than a single test print.

I rarely ran into print issues, but when I did, the AI detection worked well, pausing prints and allowing me to clear debris or cancel the job without wasting more filament.

One of the previous drawbacks of the Snapmaker U1 ecosystem at launch was that it lacked an online model repository. There are plenty of online communities that have grown up around the U1, such as on Facebook and Reddit, but model-sharing spaces serve as both a repository of knowledge and a way to find 3D designs built specifically for your machine, keeping tinkering to a minimum.

Happily, the brand has finally addressed this, launching Snapmaker Space, which is currently in open beta. If you buy this printer, it’s definitely worth checking out. It doesn’t have a community section yet, and I’m hopeful it will be added soon. After all, areas where makers can share ideas and test designs are exactly what creates innovation.

Given its four-headed design and some innovative software, the Snapmaker U1 is my go-to recommendation for anyone who wants a user-friendly option to regularly print multiple colors or materials. The U1 is beautifully designed and the user interface is a genuine pleasure to use, and its combination of performance and quality design makes it a great choice for a majority of users. Its competitors are more expensive or more difficult to use, making the U1 the natural choice for makers who want a balance of price and multicolor performance.

There are exceptions, of course. For example, a printer like the Creality K2 Pro Combo makes more sense if you’re planning to work with engineering-grade filaments like PC (polycarbonate) or ASA (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate), since you’ll need a filtered ventilation system and the higher temperatures that come with active chamber heating. (Though that will also push the retail price up more than $1,000.) On the other hand, at $750, the Snapmaker U1 may be a bit pricey for new makers: If you’re on a tighter budget, I’d recommend looking at options like the Elegoo Centauri Carbon, a single-head printer that starts at less than $300, and features a multicolor add-on.

Still, the U1 is a stellar all-around pick that delivers great performance, especially if you’re working with multiple colors. After a year, it has become one of my go-to printers across the board. Whether you’re printing a cute multicolor fidget spinner for your kids or assembling prototypes to impress investors, this is a printer capable of turning your vision into reality.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.

Every year, the Royal Meteorological Society's Weather Photographer of the Year competition offers a reminder that some of the world's most compelling images emerge from the unpredictable forces of nature. The 2026 short list includes 30 photographs selected from more than 5,500 entries submitted by photographers around the world. Each offers a different perspective into the relationship among weather, landscapes and the people who experience these natural phenomena.

The short-listed images span a range of settings and subjects, from lightning strikes, to cloud swirls, to rainbows. You can explore the full short list and vote for your favorite photo before the competition ends on Thursday (Nov. 5).

Live Science rounded up seven images that stood out for their composition, atmosphere and ability to tell a story. Which one is your favorite? Let us know in the comments!

Photographer Lisa K. Kuhn captured a lenticular cloud above Mount Shasta in California.

Watching from Bayonne, New Jersey, photographer Dan Martland captured this triple lightning strike above New York City.

"Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night," said photographer Laura Hedien about seeing this storm in Nebraska.

During a walk in England's Lake District, photographer Mat Robinson waited in the pouring rain and eventually took this image of a beautiful rainbow.

Photographer Erfan Samanfar snapped a haunting image of a farmer trying to protect his farmland from a raging fire in Marvdasht, Iran.

#6354. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.
